attacks.name: Labelled linear adapter in front of a smuggled frozen CNN (basis-recovery-free)
attacks.mechanism: No basis recovery is needed at all. A CNN on pixels is f_cnn(A^{-1} z + mu); the attacker ships only f_cnn (frozen) and learns the 81x81 (or k x 81) adapter R in-competition from the 10,000 labels by backprop through the frozen net. That is 6,561 free parameters against 10,000 labelled examples and a strongly structured loss surface, and it is exactly the regime where a good prior on f_cnn pays for itself. The smuggled artifact can be tiny: an 8-filter 3x3 first layer is 72 numbers, a usable 3-layer int8 CNN for 9x9 digits is 3-8 KB, so the ~20 KB source cap is not a binding defence against spatial-prior smuggling, only against smuggling a large model. Initialisation matters more than capacity: initialise R from any unsupervised estimate (attacks below), or from R = (pool-covariance whitener)^{-1} composed with a random rotation, then anneal. Because it never touches Q, it is invariant to rotation-only, whiten+rotate with any eps, PCA truncation (adapter becomes k->81), and separate whitening (fit the adapter on train, and the train/test map mismatch is a few-percent perturbation).
attacks.expected_effect: Recovers nothing interpretable but may recover the *benefit* of the smuggled prior, which is what the competition actually cares about. The realistic outcome is somewhere between 'converges to a generic 2-layer MLP, no gain' and 'the frozen convolutional prior plus 6.5k learned parameters beats a from-scratch MLP at fixed energy'. At 9x9 with 10k samples the MLP/CNN gap is itself modest, so the measurable quantity is small and must be measured against the honest baseline, not against chance. With 10k labels, 81 dims, the adapter is well-determined statistically (10k >> 6.5k only by 1.5x, so expect it to need weight decay / low-rank or orthogonal parametrisation of R).
attacks.runtime_cost: ~1-3 s on an A100 (200 epochs of 10k x 81 through a <20k-param net). Offline artifact 3-8 KB int8 CNN weights, well inside a 20 KB cap; a first-layer-only smuggle is 0.1 KB.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
cnn = load_int8_smuggled()          # frozen, trained offline on 9x9 pixel MNIST
R = nn.Linear(k, 81, bias=True)      # 6.5k params, the only trainable tensor
nn.init.orthogonal_(R.weight); R.weight.data *= scale_guess
opt = Adam(R.parameters(), 3e-3)
for ep in range(200):
    for zb, yb in loader(train_z, train_y, bs=256):
        xhat = R(zb).view(-1,1,9,9)
        loss = ce(cnn(xhat), yb) + lam*relu(-xhat).pow(2).mean()   # nonneg prior helps
        loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
pred = cnn(R(test_z).view(-1,1,9,9)).argmax(1)
# ablations: (a) random-init R, (b) R init from ICA attack, (c) unfreeze cnn (= honest)
attacks.how_to_measure: Query error % of {frozen-CNN + learned adapter} vs three references measured at equal wall-clock/energy: (i) honest MLP on released z, (ii) from-scratch CNN on oracle pixels (upper bound), (iii) from-scratch MLP-with-same-param-count. The defence only fails if (i) is beaten by a clear margin (>= 0.5 pp at the 2-3% error bands). Also log how close the composite R@A lands to a signed permutation - it will probably NOT be close, which is the interesting result.

attacks.name: Informed eigen-matching + class-moment refinement (kills rotation-only exactly)
attacks.mechanism: With W = I the released covariance is Q Sigma Q^T, so eigendecomposing the sample covariance of the 20k released rows gives V_z with V_z = Q V_x D for a sign diagonal D, wherever eigenvalues are separated. The attacker holds V_x, Lambda from the 60k public pool offline. Sign ambiguity is fixed by matching per-component skewness (pixel-space PC projections are strongly skewed) against the offline table. Near-degenerate eigenvalue blocks - where the gap falls below ||Sigma_hat - Sigma||_2 ~ lambda_1 sqrt(d/n) = lambda_1 sqrt(81/20000) = 0.064 lambda_1 - are not resolved by covariance alone, but the attacker also has 10,000 *labels*: the 10 released class means m_c = Q(mu_c - mu) give 9 exact linear constraints on Q (fixing Q on a 9-dim subspace outright), and the 10 released class covariances Q Sigma_c Q^T give a hugely overdetermined joint-diagonalisation problem that resolves every remaining block. Finish with orthogonal Procrustes on all the matched objects.
attacks.expected_effect: Essentially exact recovery of Q. Top ~20 eigen-directions (85-90% of the trace) are recovered from the covariance alone; class means + 10 class covariances fix the rest. Reconstruction x_hat = V_x D V_z^T z should be accurate to a few percent relative error, and an offline-trained pixel CNN applied to x_hat should land within ~0.5 pp of its accuracy on true pixels. This is the decisive evidence that rotation alone is not enough.
attacks.runtime_cost: < 5 ms on CPU (one 81x81 eigh, ten 81x81 covariances, one Procrustes). Offline artifact: V_x int8 (6.6 KB) + Lambda (0.16 KB) + skew signs (0.08 KB) + a smuggled classifier (0.8 KB) ~ 7.7 KB, inside the 20 KB cap.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
S = np.cov(z_all.T); lam_z, Vz = eigh(S)                 # released
lam_x, Vx = OFFLINE_EIG                                   # smuggled int8
ord_z, ord_x = argsort(-lam_z), argsort(-lam_x)
Vz, Vx = Vz[:,ord_z], Vx[:,ord_x]
sk = ((z_all @ Vz)**3).mean(0); Vz *= np.sign(sk*OFFLINE_SKEW_SIGN)
Q0 = Vz @ Vx.T                                            # first estimate
# refine with labels: match released class means & class covariances
M_z = stack([z_tr[y==c].mean(0) for c in range(10)])      # 10 x 81
M_x = OFFLINE_CLASS_MEANS - OFFLINE_MEAN
Q = procrustes(concat([M_x, (Q0.T@M_z.T).T]), concat([M_x, M_x]))  # or joint-diag
x_hat = z @ Q + mu_offline;  pred = smuggled_cnn(x_hat)
attacks.how_to_measure: Frobenius error ||Q_hat - Q||_F / 9; per-pixel reconstruction R^2 of x_hat vs true pixels (report per eigen-rank band); end-to-end query error of the frozen offline pixel CNN on x_hat vs on true pixels. Run once with only-covariance and once with covariance+labels to separate the two mechanisms.

attacks.name: Blind sparse-precision basis recovery on the orthogonal group (rotation-only)
attacks.mechanism: topology.py already shows that in the pixel basis the precision matrix of (sqrt-stabilised) 9x9 pixels is essentially supported on lattice edges: ~5 non-zeros per row out of 81, edge precision >= 0.99. Under rotation-only the attacker sees Sigma_z = Q Sigma Q^T, so they can search directly for the rotation that makes the precision matrix sparse: maximise over R in O(81) the sparsity of (R Sigma_z R^T)^{-1}, e.g. minimise sum_{i!=j} |P_ij| / ||P||_F with P = (R Sigma_z^{-1} ... ) computed as R Theta_z R^T where Theta_z = inv(Sigma_z + ridge I). This is a Riemannian optimisation in 3,240 parameters with a smooth objective and an extremely peaked optimum (the true basis is the unique very-sparse representation of a lattice GMRF up to signed permutation). Add a nonnegativity penalty on R z + c to break sign/scale. Once R is found, hand the output straight to topology.recover_layout, which is already measured to place every active pixel exactly at n=1,000. Critically: after whitening this objective becomes exactly flat (Sigma_z = I, precision = I for every R), which is the clean demonstration that whitening is doing the load-bearing work.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect good-to-excellent recovery for the blind attacker against rotation-only: the objective's global optimum is the pixel basis, and with n=20,000 the covariance is estimated to ~6% operator-norm accuracy, far better than needed for an L1 sparsity criterion. Main risk is local minima in 3,240 dimensions; mitigate with 20-50 restarts and a homotopy on the ridge. Once the basis is within ~0.8 matched energy per row, recover_layout should snap to the exact lattice. Predicted end-to-end: blind attacker reaches near-oracle CNN accuracy on rotation-only. Under whiten+rotate this attack must score exactly at the null.
attacks.runtime_cost: ~2-10 s on an A100 (500 Riemannian-gradient steps on an 81x81 matrix, 50 restarts, all tiny matmuls) or ~60 s CPU. Offline artifact: zero bytes (blind).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Sz = cov(z_all); Th = inv(Sz + 1e-4*I)
best = None
for restart in range(50):
    R = haar(81, seed=restart); R = torch.tensor(R, requires_grad=True)
    for it in range(500):
        P = R @ Th @ R.T
        off = P - torch.diag(torch.diag(P))
        loss = off.abs().sum()/P.norm() + lam*relu(-(z@R.T + c)).pow(2).mean()
        g = grad(loss, R); R = retract_stiefel(R, -eta*(g - R@g.T@R))  # Cayley/QR
    track best loss
feats = positive_part_features(z_all @ R_best.T)
layout = topology.recover_layout(feats)   # then cnn-09 on the layout
attacks.how_to_measure: Mean/median peak energy fraction and Hungarian matched energy of M = R_best @ A (null = 1/81 = 0.0123; ZCA ceiling from composite_controls); adjacency precision of the recovered layout vs chance 144/3240 = 0.044; exact_placement_fraction_best_dihedral; end-to-end cnn-09 query error. Report the same objective value achieved under whiten+rotate to confirm the landscape is flat there.

attacks.name: Known-marginal matching on O(81) (informed, survives whitening)
attacks.mechanism: Whitening removes second-order information but the attacker can always self-whiten anyway, so the residual secret in every variant is exactly 'an unknown rotation of the canonically whitened data'. An informed attacker knows the canonical whitened variables u = W(x - mu) offline (W is a published or self-derivable protocol object), including each u_j's full 1-D marginal. Then z = Q u and the attack is: find R in O(81) and a matching pi such that the empirical marginal of (R z)_j equals the known marginal of u_{pi(j)}. This does NOT assume independence - which is exactly where FastICA fails, since pixels are strongly dependent - it only uses the 81 known univariate laws, and those laws are highly individuated at 9x9 (a corner pixel is a delta at 0; a centre pixel is broad and bimodal). Optimise a smooth divergence (binned cross-entropy or 1-D Wasserstein to the reference CDFs) by Riemannian gradient descent on the orthogonal group, alternating with a Hungarian re-matching of coordinates to reference marginals. Only 2.6 KB of smuggled histograms are needed (81 x 32 bins int8).
attacks.expected_effect: This is my pick for the strongest informed attack that does not need the exact source images. The objective has the true Q as a global optimum with no independence assumption, and 20k samples give histogram estimates with ~0.7% bin noise, far below the between-pixel differences. Risk: heavy local-minimum structure on SO(81) and near-exchangeable marginals among symmetric pixels (the dihedral ambiguity plus left/right pixel pairs), so expect a solution correct up to a dihedral symmetry and some swapping among statistically similar pixels - which a CNN does not care about. Should partially transfer to a held-out 9x9 digit draw, because the dominant marginal structure (black frame, bright centre, zero-inflation gradient) transfers.
attacks.runtime_cost: ~1-2 s on an A100 (500 steps x 20k x 81 x 81 matmul = ~130 GFLOP total). Offline artifact: 81 x 32-bin int8 histograms = 2.6 KB, plus W or Sigma int8 = 6.6 KB.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
H_ref = SMUGGLED_HISTS                      # 81 x 32, per-pixel CDF of whitened u
Z = whiten_self(z_all)                      # attacker's own whitening -> isotropic
R = torch.tensor(haar(81), requires_grad=True)
for it in range(500):
    Y = Z @ R.T                             # 20k x 81
    H = soft_hist(Y, bins, tau=0.05)        # differentiable binned marginals
    C = wasserstein1_matrix(H, H_ref)       # 81 x 81 cost
    rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(C.detach())   # re-match every 25 steps
    loss = C[rows, cols].sum()
    R = retract_stiefel(R, -eta*riemannian_grad(loss, R))
u_hat = Z @ R.T; u_hat = u_hat[:, invperm(cols)]
x_hat = u_hat @ W_inv.T + mu; pred = smuggled_cnn(x_hat)
attacks.how_to_measure: Same localisation metrics on M = R@A (peak energy fraction, Hungarian matched energy, bijection flag) plus per-pixel Spearman correlation between x_hat and true pixels; end-to-end frozen-CNN error. Crucially also run it on a held-out non-MNIST 9x9 digit draw with MNIST-derived histograms, to measure how much of the attack survives the organizer's planned hold-out.

attacks.name: Class-conditional joint diagonalisation (informed, uses the 10k labels)
attacks.mechanism: Whitening only sterilises the *marginal* covariance. Conditional on a class, Cov(x | c) != Sigma, so Cov(z | c) = Q B_c Q^T with B_c = W Sigma_c W^T computable offline from public MNIST. The attacker has 10,000 labelled released rows, i.e. ~1,000 per class, and forms 10 released class covariances plus 10 released class means. Solving min_Q sum_c ||Q B_c Q^T - C_hat_c||_F^2 (approximate joint diagonalisation / a Procrustes on stacked eigenbases, or Riemannian descent) is massively overdetermined: 10 x 3,321 matrix entries plus 9 exact mean constraints against 3,240 unknowns. Per-class covariance noise is relative ~sqrt(81/1000) = 0.28 per entry, but averaging over 10 classes and 3,321 entries per class reduces the effective noise on Q by ~sqrt(33210/3240) = 3.2x. This is the attack that specifically defeats the 'Cov(z) = I so there are zero bits about Q' argument: there are zero bits in the *unconditional* covariance only.
attacks.expected_effect: Strong when the competition draw shares class-conditional structure with public MNIST - which is true by construction if the draw is from the pool, and largely true for any other area-resized 9x9 digit set. Expect Q recovered to within a few degrees on the well-conditioned directions and poorly on the directions where B_c ~ I for all c (the near-isotropic residual subspace). I would predict matched-energy of the composite in the 0.4-0.8 range and an end-to-end frozen-CNN error within 1-3 pp of the oracle. Weakness: it needs the class semantics to be stable, so an organizer-side random relabelling does NOT stop it (Hungarian on class covariances recovers the label map, exactly as the 1.8 KB unpermute demo already does).
attacks.runtime_cost: ~50-200 ms on an A100 (ten 81x81 covariances + a few hundred Riemannian steps). Offline artifact: 10 class covariances would be 10 x 3321 int8 = 33 KB - over cap - so ship instead the top-8 eigenpairs per class (10 x 8 x 81 int8 = 6.5 KB) or a shared 81x81 basis plus per-class spectra (~8 KB).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Chat = [cov(z_tr[y_tr==c].T) for c in range(10)]
B    = [reconstruct_lowrank(SMUGGLED_EIG[c]) for c in range(10)]   # W Sigma_c W^T
Q = torch.tensor(haar(81), requires_grad=True)
for it in range(400):
    loss = sum(((Q @ B[c] @ Q.T) - Chat[c]).pow(2).sum() for c in range(10))
    loss = loss + beta*sum(((Q @ mB[c]) - mhat[c]).pow(2).sum() for c in range(10))
    Q = retract_stiefel(Q, -eta*riemannian_grad(loss, Q))
# label permutation: Hungarian on the fitted per-class residuals, as in unpermute_demo
x_hat = (z @ Q) @ W_inv.T + mu
attacks.how_to_measure: Matched energy of Q_hat^T Q; end-to-end frozen-CNN error; and an ablation with 1k / 3k / 10k labelled rows to find the sample-size threshold. Also run the *blind* version (joint-diagonalise released class covariances against each other with a lattice-structure prior instead of offline B_c) to see whether labels alone, without public MNIST, suffice.

attacks.name: Zero-atom / cone-facet hunting via L1 hyperplane fitting (nonnegativity)
attacks.mechanism: Every variant is an invertible (or near-invertible) linear map, and a linear map preserves the geometry of the support. MNIST 9x9 pixels are area averages of ~9.7 raw pixels, so pixel p is *exactly* zero for a large fraction of images (100% for corners, 70-95% for the border ring, plausibly 10-40% for the inner ring). Each such event set {x : x_p = 0} maps to a hyperplane in released space carrying thousands of samples exactly on it. So the attacker searches for unit v and offset c such that |v.z_i - c| < tol for an anomalously large number of rows: minimise sum_i |v.z_i - c| by IRLS / L1 (the L1 minimiser famously interpolates many points), then deflate and repeat. The correct directions are rows of a matrix proportional to A^{-T} restricted to pixel p; a random direction gives ~0 exact hits, so the contrast is essentially infinite in the noiseless case. Whitening, ZCA vs PCA, the eps floor, and PCA truncation all leave this structure intact (truncation perturbs it only by the ~1e-4 variance discarded). This is also the attack that argues for a dither defence.
attacks.expected_effect: Likely recovers the high-atom pixels cleanly and the low-atom interior pixels poorly - and unfortunately for the attacker the high-atom pixels (corners, frame) are exactly the near-constant, least useful ones. The interesting empirical question is the inner-ring zero-fraction on 9x9 area-resized MNIST; if it is >= 20% the attack recovers ~40-60 pixel axes and bootstraps the rest by lattice completion. I mark this medium confidence precisely because the payoff depends on a number nobody has measured yet: histogram P(x_p == 0) per pixel. Mitigation for the organizer is cheap and decisive: add uniform or Gaussian dither of width ~1/255 to x before the map, which annihilates every exact atom at negligible honest-accuracy cost.
attacks.runtime_cost: ~1-3 s on an A100 (81 deflation rounds x 50 IRLS iterations x a 20k x 81 matvec). Offline artifact: zero bytes.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
found = []
Z = z_all.copy()
for r in range(81):
    best = None
    for restart in range(32):
        v = randn(81); v /= norm(v); c = median(Z @ v)
        for it in range(50):                       # IRLS for min ||Zv - c||_1
            res = Z @ v - c; w = 1.0/np.maximum(abs(res), 1e-4)
            v, c = weighted_tls(Z, w)              # weighted total-least-squares
        hits = (abs(Z @ v - c) < 1e-5).sum()       # exact-atom count
        track best hits
    found.append(best_v); Z = Z - outer(Z @ best_v, best_v)   # deflate
M = stack(found) @ A            # evaluation only
# also: report the per-pixel exact-zero fraction of the raw 9x9 pool first
attacks.how_to_measure: First measure P(x_p == 0) per pixel on the 9x9 pool - that single histogram predicts the attack's ceiling. Then: number of directions whose exact-hit count exceeds a null threshold; Hungarian matched energy of the found directions against rows of A^{-T}; how many of the 63-66 *active* pixels are recovered. Re-run with dither at widths {0, 1/510, 1/255, 1/64} to draw the security/accuracy trade-off curve.

attacks.name: FastICA + sign fix + recover_layout (the obvious attack; expected to underperform)
attacks.mechanism: This is the existing attack_ica.py pipeline: run FastICA on train+query released rows, fix source signs by skewness, then feed positive-part features to topology.recover_layout. The theoretical objection is model mismatch, not sample size: ICA's identifiability theorem needs independent sources, and 9x9 pixels are very far from independent (that dependence is the whole basis of topology.py). So FastICA converges to a biased optimum no matter how many samples it gets - the ceiling is roughly the ZCA basis, which attack_ica.py itself computes as control_zca_whitening. Sample-size-wise it is fine: the rotation has d(d-1)/2 = 3,240 free angles fitted from averaged nonlinear statistics over 20,000 samples, so variance is not the binding constraint (contrast that with the full 4th-order cumulant tensor, which has 81*82*83*84/24 = 1.93M free entries and is hopeless at n = 20k). A second, fixable weakness: logcosh is tuned for heavy tails, whereas zero-inflated pixels are spiky-at-zero; a mode-seeking contrast G(u) = -exp(-u^2/2s^2) with small s, or 'cube', should do materially better.
attacks.expected_effect: I expect partial localisation well above the 1/81 = 0.0123 null but well below a signed permutation - mean peak energy fraction maybe 0.05-0.20 against a ZCA ceiling of perhaps 0.2-0.4 - and recover_layout to fail or to produce adjacency precision only modestly above the 0.044 chance level. End-to-end cnn-09 accuracy should be close to the random-layout control. Low confidence that it materially succeeds; it must still be run, because it is the first thing any entrant will try and because the contrast-function ablation is cheap.
attacks.runtime_cost: 5-30 s CPU with sklearn FastICA on 20k x 81 (already implemented); < 1 s in a GPU reimplementation. Zero-byte artifact.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
for fun in ['logcosh','cube','exp', mode_seeking(s=0.3)]:
    S, Wu, model = run_ica(z_all, fun=fun, seed=k)
    M = Wu @ A                                 # evaluation only
    rep = signed_permutation_report(M); mat = matching_report(M, active)
    feats = positive_part_features(S[:n] * norm(pinv(M), axis=0))
    layout = topology.recover_layout(feats)
    err = cnn09(feats_train, y, feats_query, layout)
# controls: random-rotation null, ZCA ceiling, oracle layout
attacks.how_to_measure: Exactly the metrics attack_ica.py already emits (mean/median peak energy fraction, matched_above_0.5/0.9, distinct_peak_pixels, adjacency_precision vs chance_adjacency_precision, exact_placement_fraction_best_dihedral, cnn_query_error_pct), swept over the contrast function, over n in {2k, 10k, 20k} to separate bias from variance, and reported against both the random-rotation null and the ZCA ceiling.

attacks.name: Nonnegative ICA / orthogonal cone fitting (Plumbley)
attacks.mechanism: A sharper cousin of FastICA that exploits the one property MNIST pixels definitely have: nonnegativity with mass arbitrarily close to zero ('well-grounded'). After the attacker's own whitening, search for the orthogonal R minimising J(R) = E[ min(Rz + c, 0)^2 ], i.e. the rotation that makes every output coordinate as nonnegative as possible. Plumbley's result says that for well-grounded independent nonnegative sources the minimisers of J over the orthogonal group are exactly the signed permutations; the independence assumption is weakened here, but the geometric content - the support cone's facets pin down the axes - is much less fragile than the independence assumption FastICA leans on, because a facet {x_p = 0} carrying thousands of samples is identifiable regardless of how correlated the pixels are. J is smooth, cheap and has a much better-conditioned landscape than kurtosis maximisation. Run it with multiple restarts, and combine with the L1 facet-hunting attack (the two have the same fixed point).
attacks.expected_effect: Should beat FastICA on the same data, because it uses a property that actually holds. Still limited by the residual whitening ambiguity: pixels are correlated, so no orthogonal rotation of white data equals the pixel basis - the reachable optimum is the ZCA-like basis and the metric ceiling is the same control_zca number. The meaningful question is whether nonnegative ICA reaches that ceiling where FastICA does not, and whether a ZCA-level basis is already enough to run recover_layout and a smuggled CNN (see the ambiguity-robust-CNN entry).
attacks.runtime_cost: ~0.5-2 s on an A100 (400 Riemannian steps, 20 restarts, each a 20k x 81 x 81 matmul). Zero-byte artifact.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Z = whiten_self(z_all)
best=None
for restart in range(20):
    R = torch.tensor(haar(81), requires_grad=True); c = torch.zeros(81, requires_grad=True)
    for it in range(400):
        Y = Z @ R.T + c
        loss = torch.clamp(Y, max=0).pow(2).mean()*81
        gR, gc = grad(loss, [R, c])
        R = retract_stiefel(R, -eta*(gR - R@gR.T@R)); c = c - eta*gc
    track best loss
M = R_best @ A; report signed_permutation_report(M), matching_report(M, active)
feats = positive_part_features(Z @ R_best.T); layout = topology.recover_layout(feats)
attacks.how_to_measure: Same localisation + adjacency + end-to-end metrics as the FastICA entry, reported head-to-head with FastICA on the identical draw and against the ZCA ceiling. Also report the final J value versus J at the oracle rotation, to separate 'optimiser failed' from 'the optimum is not the pixel basis'.

attacks.name: Topographic / energy-correlation lattice QAP (fourth-order structure survives whitening)
attacks.mechanism: Whitening forces E[z_i z_j] = delta_ij but says nothing about E[z_i^2 z_j^2]. In the pixel (or ZCA-pixel) basis the energy-correlation matrix corr(s_i^2, s_j^2) is strongly local - this is the topographic-ICA structure of natural images and of digit strokes - and it is precisely the residual the whitening argument does not touch. Two stages: (a) get an approximately localized basis by any of the ICA/nonneg-ICA attacks, (b) build K_ij = corr(s_i^2, s_j^2) and run topology.py's lattice QAP (geodesic MDS + ICP + simulated-annealing 2-opt on sum_ij S_ij adj(pi_i, pi_j)) on K instead of on the partial-correlation matrix. A stronger joint version optimises over R in O(81) and the layout pi simultaneously: maximise sum_ij K_ij(R) adj(pi_i, pi_j), i.e. find the rotation whose energy correlations look most like a 9x9 lattice. That objective directly encodes the attacker's real goal (a usable grid) rather than exact pixel identity. research/attack_ica_topographic.py is stage (a)+(b) already.
attacks.expected_effect: Adjacency recovery is a much weaker requirement than exact pixel recovery, so I expect this to beat the exact-localisation metrics: plausibly adjacency precision 0.15-0.5 against the 0.044 chance level even when matched energy is only ~0.1. Whether that converts into CNN accuracy is the real question - a layout with 30% correct edges gives a CNN a badly scrambled receptive field. The joint (R, pi) version is the one I would bet on, and it is also the version nobody has run.
attacks.runtime_cost: Stage (b) alone: ~15-70 s CPU (topology.recover_layout costs 12 s laptop / 65 s scipy-free). Joint version: ~10-30 s on an A100 for 200 outer steps with a 2-opt inner loop, or use a soft (Sinkhorn) relaxation of pi to keep it differentiable. Zero-byte artifact.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
def K_of(R):
    Y = (Z @ R.T); E = Y**2; E = E - E.mean(0)
    return (E.T @ E) / (norm(E,axis=0)[:,None]*norm(E,axis=0)[None,:])
# (b) fixed-basis version
layout = topology.recover_layout_from_similarity(K_of(R_ica))
# joint version, soft permutation
R = haar(81); P = sinkhorn_logits(81,81)
for it in range(200):
    Pi = sinkhorn(P, n_iter=30)
    loss = -(K_of(R) * (Pi @ ADJ @ Pi.T)).sum()
    R = retract_stiefel(R, -eta*riemannian_grad(loss,R)); P -= eta2*grad(loss,P)
layout = hungarian(sinkhorn(P))
attacks.how_to_measure: Adjacency precision and recall of the recovered lattice against the true one under the best dihedral, vs the 0.044 chance level and vs a random-layout control; exact placement fraction; and end-to-end cnn-09 error with the recovered layout, the random layout and the oracle layout as the three points that matter.

attacks.name: eps-floor tail leak: recovering the blank-frame subspace from the released covariance
attacks.mechanism: whiten.py's own docstring concedes this but understates the size. With a floor the released covariance is Q diag(lambda/(lambda+eps)) Q^T, and with eps = 1e-3 against lambda_min = 1.5e-8 the achieved variances span 1.5e-5 to ~0.9997 - five orders of magnitude, i.e. the released data is not remotely white. The top of the spectrum is genuinely unidentifiable (lambda/(lambda+eps) ~ 1 for all the informative directions), but the 17 directions below 1e-4 are recovered as an ordered, well-separated tail: their *relative* eigenvalue gaps are orders of magnitude even though their absolute variances are tiny, and float32 release (relative precision 6e-8) does not obscure a variance of 1e-5. Those 17 directions are the always-black frame and its near-duplicates, which in pixel space are close to axis-aligned - so the attacker learns ~17 near-pixel directions, i.e. the image border, which anchors orientation and gives lattice-completion seeds for everything else. A blind attacker gets the subspace; an informed one additionally knows which pixels it should be.
attacks.expected_effect: High confidence the tail subspace is recovered (the signal is enormous relative to sampling noise: to resolve two tail directions you need their released-variance gap to exceed ~sqrt(81/20000) times the local scale, and the tail gaps are relatively huge). Much lower confidence that it converts to end-to-end accuracy, because the recovered pixels are exactly the ones with no information in them. Its real value is as a seed/anchor for the other attacks and as a dihedral-symmetry breaker. Design consequence: the eps-floor variant is strictly dominated by PCA truncation, which gives exactly identity covariance on k features with no tail to leak and no amplified quantisation noise.
attacks.runtime_cost: < 5 ms (one 81x81 eigh on the released covariance). Zero-byte artifact for the blind version.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
S = cov(z_all); lam, V = eigh(S)                 # ascending
tail = V[:, lam < 0.5]                           # the eps-suppressed directions
# pixel-space evaluation (offline only): how axis-aligned is A_inv @ tail?
B = A_inv @ tail; print((B**2).max(0)/ (B**2).sum(0))
# informed: match sorted released variances to lambda/(lambda+eps) from the public pool
k_hat = argmatch(lam, OFFLINE_LAM/(OFFLINE_LAM+eps))
Q_tail = V[:, order] @ OFFLINE_U[:, k_hat].T     # Q on the tail subspace only
# then seed the marginal-matching / nonneg-ICA search from Q_tail (fix 17 axes, search 64)
attacks.how_to_measure: Principal angles between the recovered low-variance subspace and the true bottom-17 eigenspace of Sigma, and per-direction peak-energy in pixel space; then the conditional question - does seeding the marginal-matching or nonneg-ICA attack with the tail axes fixed improve its final matched energy? Sweep eps in {0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2} and compare against n_components = 64 truncation at matched honest accuracy.

attacks.name: Ambiguity-robust smuggled CNN (makes partial basis recovery sufficient)
attacks.mechanism: This is the multiplier that converts every weak attack above into a real one. The residual ambiguity after any whitened-domain attack is not 'garbage' but a structured, simulable nuisance: an unknown mixing close to ZCA, plus a dihedral symmetry, plus swapping among statistically similar pixels. The attacker trains the offline CNN not on clean 9x9 pixels but on B x for B drawn from a *simulated posterior* over that nuisance - ZCA-style local mixing, the 8 dihedral images, small random orthogonal perturbations in near-degenerate subspaces, and pixel-swap noise - so that the smuggled net is invariant to exactly what the attack cannot resolve. Equivalently, distil the frozen net into one whose first layer is a learned 81x81 adapter with a strong locality prior. Note also that a CNN is already invariant to the dihedral ambiguity that topology.py cannot break, so the attacker does not need orientation at all; and the smuggled prior can be as small as a bank of 3x3 oriented filters (72 numbers), so the 20 KB source cap does not bite.
attacks.expected_effect: Should raise the end-to-end accuracy of every partial-recovery attack substantially, and is the reason 'we only recovered the ZCA basis, not the pixels' is not a safe conclusion. My expectation: a CNN trained with ZCA-domain and dihedral augmentation loses only ~0.3-1.0 pp versus a clean pixel CNN, which means an attack that reaches the ZCA ceiling is already close to fully successful. The organizer should treat control_zca_whitening not as a comforting ceiling but as the attacker's target.
attacks.runtime_cost: Offline: minutes on any GPU. In-submission: 0 extra cost over the frozen CNN (~1-5 ms for 10k 9x9 images on an A100). Artifact 3-8 KB int8.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
# offline
for step in range(N):
    x = sample_pool_batch()                      # clean 9x9 pixels
    B = sample_nuisance()                        # ZCA_eps @ dihedral @ small_orth_perturb
    xb = (x - mu) @ B.T
    loss = ce(cnn(xb.view(-1,1,9,9)), y); step()
# in-submission, given any attack's R_hat
feat = z @ R_hat.T
feat = (feat - feat.mean(0)) / feat.std(0)       # attacker cannot know the scale
pred = cnn(feat.view(-1,1,9,9)).argmax(1)
# optional: 8-way dihedral test-time ensembling, pick by train-set agreement
attacks.how_to_measure: Take the *oracle* ZCA basis (not any attack output) and measure end-to-end query error of (a) a clean pixel CNN, (b) a nuisance-augmented CNN. The gap is the exact quantity that decides whether 'ICA only reaches the ZCA ceiling' is a defence or not. Then re-score every attack above with the augmented CNN substituted for the clean one.

attacks.name: Distribution alignment on O(81) by sliced Wasserstein / Gromov-Wasserstein
attacks.mechanism: Generalises the known norm-and-distance matching hole to the case where the competition draw is NOT the public pool. Both the offline whitened public cloud u and the released cloud z are isotropic, so they differ only by a rotation plus whatever distribution shift separates the two datasets. Find R in O(81) minimising the sliced-Wasserstein distance between {Rz} and {u}: draw a few thousand random directions per step, sort the projections of both clouds, and take the mean 1-D W2 - this is differentiable in R and its gradient is well behaved on the orthogonal group. Unlike marginal matching it uses the joint distribution, so it does not need the coordinate axes to be individuated. A Gromov-Wasserstein variant on subsampled clouds is fully rotation-blind (distance-matrix based) and gives a sample correspondence first, from which Q follows by exact Procrustes on 81+ matched pairs.
attacks.expected_effect: If the draw IS from the public pool this recovers Q to machine precision via the GW/Procrustes route (the known hole, but note it recovers Q exactly, not merely the labels). For a held-out different-9x9-dataset draw, sliced-Wasserstein alignment degrades gracefully: it will find a rotation aligning the coarse shape of the two clouds (which is dominated by shared digit structure), plausibly giving matched energy 0.2-0.5 - enough to seed the marginal-matching or ambiguity-robust-CNN pipeline. Main obstacle is the O(81) landscape and the intrinsic near-symmetries of an isotropic cloud.
attacks.runtime_cost: Sliced-W: ~2-5 s on an A100 (300 steps x 4096 slices x 20k-element sorts). GW on 2,000 x 2,000 subsamples with entropic regularisation: ~5-20 s on an A100. Artifact: a compressed reference cloud - a 24-component GMM in the whitened domain (24 x 81 int8 means + shared diag = ~2 KB) or 200 int8 archetypes (~16 KB, at the cap).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
U = sample_reference(2000)        # from smuggled GMM/archetypes, whitened domain
R = torch.tensor(haar(81), requires_grad=True)
for it in range(300):
    theta = randn(4096, 81); theta /= theta.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True)
    a = torch.sort((Z @ R.T) @ theta.T, dim=0).values      # n x 4096
    b = torch.sort(U @ theta.T, dim=0).values
    b = interp_to_len(b, a.shape[0])
    loss = (a - b).pow(2).mean()
    R = retract_stiefel(R, -eta*riemannian_grad(loss, R))
# GW variant: soft correspondence T = entropic_gw(pdist(Z_sub), pdist(U_sub)); Q = procrustes(Z_sub, T @ U_sub)
attacks.how_to_measure: Run twice: once with the draw taken from the public pool (expect near-exact Q, confirming the hole) and once on the planned held-out 9x9 dataset (the number that actually matters). Metrics: ||Q_hat^T Q - I||_F, matched energy, and end-to-end error with the ambiguity-robust CNN. Report the sliced-W loss at the oracle rotation as the achievable floor.

attacks.name: Adjacency-only recovery feeding a graph/permutation-equivariant learner
attacks.mechanism: The attacker does not need an embedding into a 9x9 grid, only a neighbourhood graph: a graph-convolution or set-transformer with smuggled, locality-shaped weights works on any adjacency structure, and message passing on the recovered edge set reproduces most of what a CNN's inductive bias buys. Recovering *edges* is a far lower bar than recovering the *layout*: topology.py's own pipeline spends most of its machinery (geodesic MDS, ICP, QAP annealing) turning a good k-NN graph into a grid embedding, and the k-NN graph from energy correlations survives much more noise than the embedding does. So: run any of the basis attacks, build the energy-correlation matrix, take the mutual-4-NN graph, discard the embedding step entirely, and run a smuggled GNN. Additionally, even a *wrong* but locally-consistent graph gives a useful sparse prior compared to a dense MLP.
attacks.expected_effect: Should be the most robust residual attack under weak basis recovery, because it degrades smoothly: adjacency precision 0.3 still produces a graph with real locality. Whether it beats an honest MLP at 9x9 with 10k samples is uncertain and is the key measurement; my prior is that at this resolution the CNN-over-MLP gap is small anyway, so this may 'succeed' as an attack while being worthless as a leaderboard advantage.
attacks.runtime_cost: ~1-5 s on an A100 for the graph build plus a small GNN. Artifact: a locality-shaped GNN, 2-6 KB int8.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
S = R_hat_output_sources                # from ICA / nonneg-ICA / any attack
E = (S**2); E -= E.mean(0)
K = corrcoef(E.T)
nbr = mutual_knn(K, k=4)                # symmetric 4-NN, no embedding step
edges = to_edge_index(nbr)
net = load_smuggled_gnn()               # frozen conv weights, learned readout
train_readout(net, S_train, y_train, edges)
pred = net(S_query, edges).argmax(1)
# controls: random 4-regular graph, oracle lattice graph, dense MLP
attacks.how_to_measure: Adjacency precision/recall of the recovered mutual-kNN graph vs the true lattice (chance 0.044); then end-to-end query error of the GNN on {recovered graph, random 4-regular graph, oracle lattice}. The gap between the oracle-graph GNN and the honest MLP is the upper bound on what any graph-level attack can possibly buy - measure that first, it may be near zero.

attacks.name: Separate train/test whitening: Wishart-discrepancy leak (expected to fail, but the variant is harmful anyway)
attacks.mechanism: If train and test are whitened with their own statistics under a shared Q, the composite discrepancy D = A_te A_tr^{-1} = Q Sigma_te^{-1/2} Sigma_tr^{1/2} Q^T is estimable by the attacker (align the two released clouds' covariances). D - I is the Wishart sampling fluctuation, whose covariance structure is Cov(dSigma_ij, dSigma_kl) = (Sigma_ik Sigma_jl + Sigma_il Sigma_jk)/n - i.e. it is generated by Sigma in the *pixel* basis, so in principle it leaks Sigma and therefore the lattice. In practice the attacker observes exactly one realisation: 3,321 numbers constraining 3,321 unknowns of Sigma, with no averaging available, so the estimate is hopeless unless Sigma is given a low-dimensional lattice parametrisation - and choosing among 81! layouts by likelihood is infeasible. I include it because it is the obvious 'does separate whitening leak?' question and it should be measured and dismissed. Separately and more importantly, separate whitening is self-defeating for honest reasons: with n = 10,000 and d = 81 the two whiteners differ by ~sqrt(81/10000) = 9% in covariance / ~4.5% in the map, which is a pure train-test distribution shift that costs honest accuracy; and a learner can partly undo it by re-whitening both splits itself, so it buys no obfuscation. If Q also differs between splits, every learner including a linear one fails completely.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect no usable recovery from the discrepancy (that is the point of listing it). Expect a small but measurable honest-accuracy cost from the train/test mismatch, and a catastrophic one if Q differs. Recommendation ahead of the measurement: one shared map, fitted on the pool or on the union of the released train and test rows.
attacks.runtime_cost: < 10 ms to estimate D; any serious inference from it is the expensive-and-futile part. Zero-byte artifact.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Str = cov(z_train.T); Ste = cov(z_test.T)
D = sqrtm(Ste) @ inv(sqrtm(Str))            # ~ Q Sigma_te^-1/2 Sigma_tr^1/2 Q^T
Delta = D - I
# test for leakage: is any rotation R making R Delta R^T look lattice-structured?
for restart in range(50):
    R = haar(81); optimise sparsity/locality of R @ Delta @ R.T
# null: repeat with Delta drawn from a Wishart fluctuation of an isotropic Sigma
# honest cost, measured separately:
#   err(shared map) vs err(separate W, shared Q) vs err(separate W, separate Q)
attacks.how_to_measure: Compare the best achievable locality score of R Delta R^T against a null where Delta is generated from an isotropic Sigma; if the two distributions overlap, no leak. In parallel run E3 as designed: honest MLP / linear / CNN query error under shared-map vs separate-W-shared-Q vs separate-W-separate-Q, at n = 10,000.

attacks.name: Quantisation-lattice reduction (exotic, expected to fail, motivates the dither defence)
attacks.mechanism: 9x9 area resizing of uint8 MNIST with 28/9 box weights makes every pixel value an integer multiple of 1/(28*255) = 1/7140, so raw x lives on the lattice (1/7140) Z^81 and the released z lives on the image of that lattice under A. Float32 release quantises at ~6e-8 relative, far finer than the induced lattice spacing (1.4e-4 / sqrt(lambda), i.e. ~1.4e-4 for unit-variance directions), so the lattice is *visible* in the released numbers. Recovering a basis of a lattice from samples is lattice reduction (LLL/BKZ), which returns a basis up to a unimodular transform; the pixel basis is the natural one in raw space but after whitening it is badly skewed, so the reduced basis will generally not be the pixel basis. I rate this low confidence but it is worth a cheap check because it is the kind of thing a determined entrant finds, and because the mitigation - dithering x by ~U(0, 1/255) before the map - simultaneously kills this attack and the zero-atom facet attack.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect failure at d = 81 with a whitening-induced condition number of ~1e4 (LLL's approximation factor is exponential in the dimension). The one sub-case worth a look: the *differences* z_i - z_j between images that agree on many pixels, which are short vectors of the lattice and could expose a few basis directions directly. Even a negative result is valuable because it justifies not adding dither, if the zero-atom attack also fails.
attacks.runtime_cost: LLL on an 81-dim basis with fpylll: seconds to minutes offline; not runnable inside a scored submission in any case (so this is an offline-only attack that outputs a fixed A_hat, which only works if A is reused across draws - another argument for a fresh Q per draw). Zero-byte artifact if A is per-draw secret; then the attack is dead.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
# only meaningful if the same A is reused across draws / is offline-inferable
Diffs = z[idx_a] - z[idx_b]                     # candidate short lattice vectors
Diffs = Diffs[norm(Diffs, axis=1) < q]          # keep the shortest
B = lattice_basis_from_generators(Diffs)        # HNF / integer relation
B_red = LLL(B, delta=0.99)                      # or BKZ-20
M = B_red @ A_inv                               # evaluation only: is it unimodular*perm?
# defence check: repeat after adding dither u ~ U(0, 1/255) to x before the map
attacks.how_to_measure: Histogram the released values of a single coordinate at high resolution and look for comb structure; check whether the shortest recovered lattice vectors align with columns of A. Then measure the honest-accuracy cost of dithering at widths {1/510, 1/255, 1/64} so the organizer has the price of closing both this and the zero-atom hole.

red:ml-signal.defence_notes:
STRUCTURAL POINT THAT REORGANISES THE WHOLE QUESTION. The attacker can always whiten the released data themselves. Therefore, for every variant, the residual secret is exactly the same object: "an unknown rotation of the canonically whitened data". Whitening on the organizer's side contributes exactly one thing - it prevents the attacker from reading Sigma's eigenstructure in the released frame - and nothing else. Consequences: (a) W is not, and cannot be, a secret, so publishing it costs nothing and hiding it buys nothing; (b) ZCA vs PCA is a non-choice once Q is Haar (whiten.py already proves Q W_zca = (QU) W_pca with QU Haar) - the only real knobs are eps and k; (c) rotation-only is broken twice over (informed: eigen-matching + class moments, ~exact, confidence 0.95; blind: sparse-precision basis recovery, confidence 0.6), so the answer to Q1 is that rotation alone is NOT enough and whitening is mandatory.

ANSWER TO Q2 (separate vs joint whitening): use ONE shared map. Separate whitening buys no obfuscation (the attacker self-whitens regardless), costs honest accuracy through a ~4.5% train/test map mismatch at n=10,000 (sqrt(81/10000) covariance error), is partially undoable by an honest learner re-whitening both splits, opens a small theoretical Wishart-discrepancy leak, and is catastrophic if Q also differs per split (no learner, not even linear, transfers). Fit the map on the pool, or on the union of the released train+test rows; both are fine and the union version removes the "must publish a pool-derived object" awkwardness.

THE eps-FLOOR VARIANT IS STRICTLY DOMINATED. With eps=1e-3 against lambda_min=1.5e-8 the achieved variances lambda/(lambda+eps) span 1.5e-5 to 0.9997, so the released covariance is nowhere near the identity and the bottom-17 (blank-frame) directions are handed over exactly, while the informative top of the spectrum stays hidden. PCA truncation to k ~ 64 (drop lambda < 1e-4) gives exactly identity covariance on the released features, no tail to leak, and no amplified area-resize quantisation noise. If the whiten+rotate family is used at all, use n_components=k, not an eps floor. eps=0 with 81 features is the other defensible corner but it releases ~17 coordinates of pure quantisation noise.

WHAT WHITENING DOES NOT REMOVE, ranked by how much I would worry:
1. Class-conditional second-order structure. Cov(z | class c) = Q W Sigma_c W^T Q^T is not the identity and the attacker has 10,000 labels. Joint diagonalisation against offline class covariances is massively overdetermined (10 x 3,321 equations for 3,240 unknowns) and is my highest-confidence attack against whiten+rotate (0.8). Nothing in the current defence addresses it. Label-permuting the classes does not help - the 1.8 KB unpermute demo already recovers a label map by Hungarian matching.
2. Known univariate marginals. Whitening changes the marginals but an informed attacker can compute the whitened-domain marginals offline; matching 81 known 1-D laws over O(81) needs NO independence assumption, which is exactly where FastICA is fundamentally handicapped (pixels are dependent by construction - that dependence is what topology.py exploits).
3. Support geometry: nonnegativity and exact-zero atoms. Any invertible linear map preserves them. The single most informative unmeasured number in this whole design is the per-pixel exact-zero fraction P(x_p = 0) on the 9x9 area-resized pool - measure it before anything else, it sets the ceiling for the cone/facet attacks and tells you whether dithering is worth its accuracy cost.
4. Fourth-order / energy-correlation (topographic) structure, which is local in the pixel basis and is the only thing the existing ICA attacks are really chasing.

DO NOT TREAT control_zca_whitening AS A SAFE CEILING. attack_ica.py frames the ZCA basis as "the best any ICA-style attack could hope to return", implying that falling short of pixels means safety. It does not: an attacker can train the offline CNN on deliberately ZCA-mixed, dihedrally-augmented, orthogonally-perturbed inputs so that the smuggled prior is invariant to exactly the ambiguity the attack cannot resolve. Please measure the end-to-end error of a nuisance-augmented CNN given the ORACLE ZCA basis - that single number tells you whether "ICA only reaches ZCA" is a defence or a formality.

THE SIZE CAP IS NOT A DEFENCE AGAINST FEATURE SMUGGLING. An 8-filter 3x3 edge bank is 72 numbers; a usable int8 9x9 CNN is 3-8 KB; the informed-attack artifacts sketched above (eigenbasis 6.6 KB int8, per-pixel histograms 2.6 KB, low-rank class covariances 6.5 KB) all fit inside 20 KB. The cap only stops smuggling a large model.

THE EXPERIMENT I WOULD RUN FIRST, BEFORE ANY ATTACK. Measure the honest CNN-over-MLP gap at 9x9 with 10,000 training samples, at matched energy/time, at each accuracy band. At this resolution the spatial prior may be worth very little; if the oracle-layout CNN beats the best MLP by, say, under 0.3 pp, the entire feature-smuggling threat is economically dead and no obfuscation is needed. Every attack above should be scored against that gap, not against chance - "recovered the lattice" and "gained leaderboard position" are different events and only the second one matters. The corresponding hard upper bound for the graph-level attacks is the oracle-lattice-GNN vs dense-MLP gap.

DESIGN LEVERS THAT ACTUALLY BITE, in rough order of cost-effectiveness: (i) fresh secret Q (and mu, W) per draw, so no offline-computed A_hat is reusable and every attack must run inside the scored submission's seconds; (ii) a held-out non-public draw, which is the only thing that kills the exact-sample-matching / Procrustes hole and degrades the informed marginal/OT attacks to partial; (iii) small dither (~U(0,1/255)) on x before the map, which annihilates the exact-zero atoms and the quantisation lattice at a measurable and probably tiny accuracy cost - price it; (iv) PCA truncation instead of an eps floor; (v) accept that a *labelled* 81x81 adapter in front of a frozen smuggled CNN is invariant to every linear release map, and defend that case by evaluation design (ranked hold-out, per-draw secrets, energy accounting that charges for the adapter's training) rather than by obfuscation. Linear release maps cannot stop attack #1 in the list, by construction - that is the single most important thing to measure and, if it succeeds, the whole "decorrelate and rotate" line of defence should be abandoned in favour of evaluation-side controls.

attacks.name: Self-whitening reduction (the lemma that ranks the variants)
attacks.mechanism: Let the release be z = Q W (x - mu) with W any invertible whitener (ZCA, PCA, eps-floored, or rank-k). The attacker computes his own whitening of the released cloud, z_hat = Cov(z)^{-1/2} (z - zbar). Then z_hat = R * Sigma^{-1/2}(x - mu) for some orthogonal R, exactly, for every choice of W: the composite Cov(z)^{-1/2} Q W has identity covariance, and any two matrices that whiten the same population differ by a left orthogonal factor. Consequently rotation-only, ZCA+eps, PCA+eps and rank-k truncation all deliver the SAME object to the attacker up to an unknown element of O(d) -- they are not different defences, they are one defence plus or minus the single second-order channel. Whitening's entire contribution is to delete the 3321 equations Cov(z) = Q Sigma Q^T; everything of order 3 and above, and everything class-conditional, is bit-for-bit identical in all variants. So whiten+rotate strictly dominates rotation-only, and no further security is bought by the choice of ZCA vs PCA (whiten.py already notes Q W_zca = (QU) W_pca with QU Haar).
attacks.expected_effect: Not a recovery attack; a normalisation that must be applied before every other attack and that predicts the E1/E2 result structure. Prediction to check: every metric in E1/E2 that is computed AFTER attacker self-whitening will be statistically identical between rotation-only and whiten+rotate (within Monte-Carlo error over rotation seeds). If the experiment reports a gap there, it is a bug or a numerical-conditioning artefact, not security. Constraint accounting for the informed attacker: unconditional covariance 3321 equations, class means 810, class-conditional covariances 33,210, third cumulants ~88k, fourth ~1.8M, versus 3240 unknowns in R. Whitening removes ~0.2% of the informed attacker's identifying equations.
attacks.runtime_cost: 1 eigh of an 81x81 matrix: <1 ms on A100, ~0.5 ms CPU. Zero offline artifact.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
C  = np.cov(z, rowvar=False)            # 81x81
d, V = np.linalg.eigh(C)
Whalf = (V * (1/np.sqrt(np.clip(d, 1e-12, None)))) @ V.T
zw = (z - z.mean(0)) @ Whalf.T          # now zw = R @ Sigma^-1/2 (x-mu)
# every subsequent attack estimates the single orthogonal R
# sanity: np.allclose(np.cov(zw, rowvar=False), np.eye(81), atol=1e-6)
# run the identical downstream attack on rotation-only and on whiten+rotate
# releases and assert the metrics agree -> confirms the variants collapse
attacks.how_to_measure: Generate both releases from the same draw and the same rotation seed, self-whiten each, and report the Frobenius distance between the two self-whitened clouds after optimal orthogonal Procrustes (they should align to ~1e-6 for eps=0, and to O(eps-induced float32 noise) otherwise). Then run every attack in this list on both and tabulate the metric gap.

attacks.name: Fixed-map fold-in: smuggle A_inv (or the composed first layer) instead of attacking
attacks.mechanism: whiten.py fits (mu, Sigma, Q) on the 60,000-image pool and describes the map as a protocol constant that 'must be published with the protocol'. If A is the same for every draw and every submission, no attack is needed at all: the attacker trains a CNN offline on public 9x9 MNIST in pixel space, then folds A^{-1} into the first layer. For a first layer that is linear in x, h = W1 x + b1 becomes h = (W1 A^{-1}) z + (b1 + W1 mu), so the smuggled artifact is only as large as the first layer, and everything after it is unchanged. Alternatively smuggle A^{-1} itself: 81x81 int8 with 81 per-row float16 scales is 6,723 bytes, comfortably inside a 20 KB source cap, and it reconstructs pixels to ~0.4% relative error (int8 on a well-conditioned matrix), after which any offline CNN runs at full pixel-space accuracy. This is the exact analogue of the measured 1.8 KB unpermute table, and it makes the rotation and the whitening decorative.
attacks.expected_effect: Full pixel recovery, hence full smuggling, at essentially zero in-submission cost and ~7 KB of source. Recovery error dominated by int8 quantisation of A^{-1}: expect reconstructed-x MSE ~1e-5 and smuggled-CNN error within 0.1 pp of the pixel-space CNN. This dominates every other attack in this list and must be closed before any of the others matter: (mu, W, Q) have to be freshly drawn per submission from a secret seed, and the transform's provenance must not be reproducible from published pool statistics.
attacks.runtime_cost: ~0 ms in submission (one 81x81 matmul, <0.05 ms on A100). Offline artifact 6.7 KB (A_inv int8) or ~2-10 KB (folded first layer, int8).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
# offline, once, knowing the published transform dict T
Ainv = T['A_inv']                     # 81x81
scale = np.abs(Ainv).max(1) / 127
q8   = np.round(Ainv / scale[:,None]).astype(np.int8)   # 6561 B + 162 B
# in submission
Ainv = q8.astype(np.float32) * scale[:,None]
x    = z @ Ainv.T + T['mean']         # pixels, up to int8 error
logits = smuggled_cnn(x.reshape(-1,1,9,9))
# variant: skip A_inv, ship W1 @ Ainv and b1 + W1 @ mean only
attacks.how_to_measure: Quantise A_inv to int8, measure reconstruction MSE against true pixels and the end-to-end error of a frozen offline CNN applied to the reconstruction; compare against the same CNN on true pixels. Also measure the byte count of the smuggled artifact. Then repeat with a per-draw fresh rotation seed to confirm the attack dies, which is the decision the organizer actually needs.

attacks.name: Second-order eigen-Procrustes with third-moment sign fixing
attacks.mechanism: For W = I the released covariance is C_z = Q Sigma Q^T. The attacker computes Sigma from the 60k public images and eigendecomposes both. If the eigenvalues are distinct, Q = V_z S V_x^T with S a diagonal of unknown signs, and the 81 signs are fixed independently by a scalar comparison: the skewness of the projection of x - mu onto eigenvector u_i is known offline and is large for MNIST (pixels are strongly right-skewed), so sign_i = sign(skew(z V_z[:,i]) * skew((x-mu) V_x[:,i])). Near-degenerate eigenvalues leave residual rotations inside their blocks; the perturbation bound is sin(theta_i) ~ ||dSigma|| / gap_i with ||dSigma||_ij ~ sqrt(lambda_i lambda_j / N), so at N = 20,000 a block is resolved whenever the relative eigengap exceeds ~1%. The degenerate blocks are exactly the low-variance blank-border directions, which the attacker does not need; the top ~30 directions carry essentially all the digit signal and have well-separated eigenvalues. Residual block rotations can then be polished by the class-mean and class-covariance Procrustes attacks below.
attacks.expected_effect: Near-complete pixel recovery for rotation-only. Expect the composite V_z S V_x^T to reconstruct x with correlation >0.98 on the ~60 active pixels and an offline pixel CNN to run within ~0.5 pp of its clean error. Rotation-only should be declared broken by this alone; it costs one eigh and 81 skewness comparisons. This is the concrete answer to organizer question (1): rotation alone is not enough.
attacks.runtime_cost: 2 eigh + 2 matmuls: ~1 ms on A100, ~5 ms CPU. Offline artifact: Sigma's eigenvectors 81x81 int8 = 6.7 KB, or only the top-30 = 2.5 KB plus 30 skewness signs.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
dz, Vz = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(z, rowvar=False))       # ascending
dx, Vx = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma_pub)                     # ascending, offline
sz = ((z @ Vz - (z@Vz).mean(0))**3).mean(0)
sx = skew_pub                                          # offline, 81 floats
S  = np.sign(sz * sx); S[S == 0] = 1
Qhat = (Vz * S) @ Vx.T                                 # z ~ Qhat @ (x-mu)
xhat = z @ Qhat + mu_pub
# optional: report per-direction |cos| between Qhat.T Vz and Vx columns
# and eigengap dx[i+1]/dx[i] - 1 to see exactly where it degrades
attacks.how_to_measure: Per-eigendirection |cos angle| between recovered and true eigenvector plotted against the relative eigengap; reconstruction R^2 per pixel; adjacency precision of topology.recover_layout run on the reconstruction; end-to-end error of a frozen offline CNN on the reconstruction versus on true pixels. Sweep N in {1k, 3k, 10k, 20k} to find the sample size at which each block resolves.

attacks.name: Class-conditional covariance Procrustes (joint-diagonalisation matching)
attacks.mechanism: This is the strongest attack that survives whitening, and it uses only second moments, so it does not depend on non-Gaussianity at all. After self-whitening, z_hat = R x_hat with x_hat = Sigma^{-1/2}(x - mu). Labels are given for 10,000 train rows, so the attacker forms the 10 class-conditional covariances A_c = Cov(z_hat | y = c) and knows the matching B_c = Cov(x_hat | y = c) offline. Whitening forces sum_c p_c (A_c + m_c m_c^T) = I but leaves each A_c free, and the constraint A_c = R B_c R^T for c = 0..9 is 10 x 3321 = 33,210 equations in 3240 unknowns -- overdetermined by a factor of ten. Degeneracy is no longer a problem: a direction is unidentifiable only if ALL ten class covariances are simultaneously degenerate in it, which for MNIST happens only in the dead-border subspace. Solve by maximising f(R) = sum_c tr(R^T A_c R B_c) over O(81) with projected gradient / polar retraction, initialised from the class-mean Procrustes below; this is an orthogonal joint-diagonalisation matching problem with a benign landscape once the 9-dimensional mean subspace is pinned.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect near-complete recovery of R on the subspace where the class covariances actually differ. MNIST class-conditional covariance differences are high rank (roughly 40-60 informative directions at 9x9), so the recovered R should reconstruct x with R^2 above ~0.9 on active pixels and let a frozen offline CNN run within 1-2 pp of pixel-space accuracy. Sampling noise is the binding constraint: each A_c is estimated from ~1000 rows for an 81x81 matrix, so entrywise relative error is ~sqrt(2/1000) ~ 4.5%; pooling ten matrices recovers roughly a factor of 3. If this attack lands, whitening is definitively not sufficient and the answer to question (3) is 'yes, the attacker still gets the pixel basis'.
attacks.runtime_cost: A_c: one batched 81x81 outer-product reduction over 10k rows, <1 ms A100. 500 Stiefel iterations x 10 restarts x 10 matrices of 81x81 matmuls: ~20 ms A100, ~2 s CPU. Offline artifact: rank-12 factors L_c (81x12) for the 10 classes, int8 = 9.7 KB, plus 810 B of class means; or full B_c int8 = 33 KB (too big, use the rank-truncated form).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
zw = selfwhiten(z_train)                       # lemma above
A  = [np.cov(zw[y==c], rowvar=False) for c in range(10)]
B  = [Lc @ Lc.T for Lc in smuggled_rank12_factors]      # offline, 9.7 KB
R  = procrustes(class_means(zw, y), smuggled_class_means)   # init, see below
for it in range(500):
    G = sum(2 * Ac @ R @ Bc for Ac, Bc in zip(A, B))    # d f / d R
    R = polar(R + lr * (G - R @ G.T @ R))               # Stiefel step
xhat = zw @ R @ Sigma_half_pub.T + mu_pub
logits = smuggled_cnn(xhat.reshape(-1,1,9,9))
# report f(R)/f(R_true) and the per-direction |cos| spectrum of R^T R_true
attacks.how_to_measure: Singular values of R_hat^T R_true (a spectrum of 81 cosines: how many directions were recovered); reconstruction R^2 per pixel; end-to-end frozen-offline-CNN error. Ablate: number of classes used (2, 5, 10), rank r of the smuggled B_c factors (4, 8, 12, 24, full), and n_train in {1k, 3k, 10k}. Also run the identical pipeline against the rotation-only release to confirm the lemma (metrics should match).

attacks.name: Class-mean orthogonal Procrustes (810-byte anchor)
attacks.mechanism: Labels supply the correspondence for free, so this is a classical Procrustes problem with 10 exact point correspondences rather than an alignment search. The attacker computes the 10 class means in self-whitened released space, m_c, and knows the 10 class means in self-whitened pixel space, n_c, offline. Then R = UV^T from the SVD of sum_c p_c m_c n_c^T. Because the 10 centred means span only 9 dimensions, R is determined exactly on a 9-dimensional subspace and is completely free on the orthogonal 72-dimensional complement. This alone is NOT a smuggling win -- a 9-dimensional discriminative subspace is just LDA, which an honest learner can fit -- but it is the correct initialiser for the class-covariance and cumulant attacks, it resolves their sign/reflection ambiguities, and it is the cheapest possible artifact (81x10 int8 = 810 bytes, exactly the table measured in the existing unpermute demo). Its value should be measured as 'does it turn a failing manifold optimisation into a succeeding one', not as a standalone recovery.
attacks.expected_effect: Exact recovery of R restricted to the 9-dimensional between-class subspace (sampling error ~ sqrt(81/1000) per class mean, so cosines >0.99). Standalone smuggled-CNN accuracy should be poor (reconstruction is rank-9); expect a reconstruction R^2 of only ~0.2-0.4 and a smuggled CNN near chance-plus. Predicted role: raises the success rate of attack #5 from restart-dependent to near-deterministic. Include it explicitly as a low-standalone-confidence entry so the experiment measures the initialiser effect rather than conflating it.
attacks.runtime_cost: One 81x10 matmul plus an SVD of an 81x81 matrix: <0.5 ms A100. Offline artifact 810 B int8 + 10 float16 scales.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
zw = selfwhiten(z_train)
M  = np.stack([zw[y==c].mean(0) for c in range(10)])       # 10x81
N  = smuggled_class_means_whitened                          # 10x81, 810 B
M -= M.mean(0); N -= N.mean(0)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M.T @ N)                           # 81x81
R0 = U @ Vt                                                 # zw ~ xw @ R0.T
# standalone reconstruction (rank-9 informative):
xhat = zw @ R0 @ Sigma_half_pub.T + mu_pub
# main use: hand R0 to attack #5 / #8 as the initialiser
attacks.how_to_measure: Report the 9 recovered cosines and the residual 72-dimensional ambiguity explicitly. Then measure attack #5's success rate (fraction of seeds reaching the global optimum of f) with random-orthogonal init versus this init, over >=20 rotation seeds. Standalone smuggled-CNN error should be reported as the expected-failure baseline.

attacks.name: FOBI / kurtosis-matrix eigen-matching
attacks.mechanism: The fourth-order contraction K = E[ ||z_hat||^2 z_hat z_hat^T ] is equivariant under the unknown rotation: K_z = R K_x R^T, and K_x is computable offline from public MNIST. So the rotation is recoverable by exactly the same eigen-Procrustes as attack #1, but with K in place of Sigma -- and K is NOT killed by whitening. This is FOBI, the cheapest possible fourth-order attack: two d x d eigendecompositions and a sign fix. Its weakness is identical to #1's: the eigenvalues of K (the generalised kurtoses) must be separated, and for whitened image data many of them cluster. The same family supplies free one-dimensional anchors: v = E[||z_hat||^2 z_hat] and E[||z_hat||^4 z_hat] are equivariant vectors, each pinning one direction exactly and each costing 81 floats to smuggle. Sign fixing uses the third moments of the released coordinates against their offline counterparts.
attacks.expected_effect: Partial recovery on its own -- expect the top ~10-20 FOBI eigendirections to be recovered with cosine >0.9 and the rest to be lost in near-degenerate clusters, since the generalised-kurtosis spectrum of whitened MNIST is not well separated. Variance of each K entry is O(1/N) with N = 20,000 plus heavy-tail inflation from the fourth moment, so effective precision is closer to N_eff ~ 2,000-5,000. Mark this as an initialiser-grade attack, expected to fail standalone; its value is as a 5-line, no-labels alternative to JADE and as a cheap R0 for #5 and #8.
attacks.runtime_cost: One weighted covariance over 20k rows + 2 eigh: ~1 ms A100, ~30 ms CPU. Offline artifact: K_x eigenvectors 81x81 int8 = 6.7 KB, or top-20 = 1.6 KB.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
zw = selfwhiten(np.concatenate([z_train, z_test]))    # 20k rows, no labels
w  = (zw**2).sum(1)                                   # ||z||^2
Kz = (zw * w[:,None]).T @ zw / len(zw)
dz, Vz = np.linalg.eigh(Kz)
dx, Vx = smuggled_Kx_eig                              # offline
S  = np.sign(((zw @ Vz)**3).mean(0) * smuggled_skew_x)
R  = (Vz * S) @ Vx.T
# diagnostic that predicts success: np.diff(dx)/dx[:-1] vs 1/sqrt(N_eff)
attacks.how_to_measure: Plot the generalised-kurtosis spectrum of whitened 9x9 MNIST and its relative gaps against the sampling floor 1/sqrt(N). Report per-direction recovery cosine against gap. Report standalone reconstruction R^2 and smuggled-CNN error, and the same after handing R to attack #5 for polish.

attacks.name: JADE / third-cumulant Procrustes on the Stiefel manifold (label-free)
attacks.mechanism: The full higher-order channel is the cumulant tensor, which transforms as T_z = (R x R x R) T_x for order 3 and analogously for order 4. Matching them directly gives an enormously overdetermined system: 81^3/6 ~ 88,000 equations at order 3 and ~1.8M at order 4, against 3240 unknowns. The practical implementation is JADE-style: build a set of cumulant matrices Q(M) = E[(z^T M z) z z^T] - M - M^T - tr(M) I for a family of probe matrices M, which satisfy Q_z(R M R^T) = R Q_x(M) R^T, and minimise sum_M || Q_z(R M R^T) - R Q_x(M) R^T ||_F^2 over R by Riemannian gradient descent with polar retraction. Unlike blind ICA this does not require the pixel basis to be the maximally-independent basis -- it only requires the two clouds to have the same distribution up to R, which is the informed attacker's exact situation when the draw comes from the same source. Probe matrices can be the 81 rank-1 e_i e_i^T plus ~100 random ones, keeping the artifact small.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect this to be the strongest label-free informed attack and comparable to #5. At 20,000 rows and 81 dimensions, third-cumulant entries have standard error ~ sqrt(Var)/sqrt(N) ~ 0.7% relative; the classical ICA sample-complexity rule N >~ 5 d^2 = 33,000 says 20k is marginal but the informed version is far better conditioned than blind ICA because it fits 3240 parameters to ~88k measured targets rather than optimising a contrast. Predict recovery of 50-70 of the 81 directions with cosine >0.9, enough for a frozen offline CNN to land within 2-4 pp of its pixel-space error. Crucially it works on a held-out draw from a different 9x9 dataset as long as the low-order cumulant structure is similar, which is what makes it more dangerous than sample matching.
attacks.runtime_cost: Cumulant matrices for 180 probes over 20k rows: ~181 batched 81x81 reductions, ~10-30 ms A100 (a few seconds CPU). 1000 Stiefel iterations: ~50 ms A100. Offline artifact: 180 Q_x(M) matrices at 81x81 int8 = 1.2 MB (too big) -- so smuggle instead the rank-truncated basis (top 16 eigenpairs per probe, 24 probes) ~ 8 KB, or smuggle only the ICA/JADE mixing matrix of the public data, 81x81 int8 = 6.7 KB, and match components.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
zw = selfwhiten(np.concatenate([z_train, z_test]))
def Qmat(Z, M):
    w = ((Z @ M) * Z).sum(1)
    return (Z * w[:,None]).T @ Z / len(Z) - M - M.T - np.trace(M)*np.eye(81)
probes = [np.eye(81)[:,[i]] @ np.eye(81)[[i],:] for i in range(81)] + rand_sym(100)
Qz = [Qmat(zw, M) for M in probes]
R  = R0_from_class_means_or_FOBI
for it in range(1000):
    loss = sum(((Qz_i - R @ Qx_i @ R.T)**2).sum() for Qz_i, Qx_i in zip(Qz, Qx))
    R = polar(R - lr * riemannian_grad(loss, R))
xhat = zw @ R @ Sigma_half_pub.T + mu_pub
attacks.how_to_measure: Recovery-cosine spectrum of R_hat^T R_true; reconstruction R^2; frozen-CNN error. Sweep N in {5k, 10k, 20k, 40k} to locate the 5d^2 threshold empirically. Critically, run it on a held-out 9x9 draw from a DIFFERENT source (e.g. EMNIST-digits or KMNIST resized) to test whether the attack survives the organizer's planned hold-out, which is the whole point of that hold-out.

attacks.name: Wasserstein / Gromov-Wasserstein Procrustes (unpaired distribution alignment)
attacks.mechanism: The released cloud and the attacker's public cloud are two independent samples from distributions related by an unknown orthogonal map. Aligning them is exactly the unsupervised-embedding-alignment problem: alternate a soft assignment (Sinkhorn on the squared-distance cost) with an orthogonal Procrustes update, initialised from Gromov-Wasserstein on the intra-cloud distance matrices (which are themselves fully Q-invariant, so GW uses only invariants and needs no anchor). This is a global method that does not depend on eigengaps, cumulant conditioning, or labels, and it is known to work in dimension 300 with 20k points in the word-embedding literature; d = 81 with 10-20k points is comfortably inside its operating range. Sub-sample to ~2,000 points per side for tractability, run 200 Sinkhorn-Procrustes iterations from ~20 restarts and keep the lowest transport cost. Unlike exact sample matching it degrades gracefully when the draw is from a different-but-similar 9x9 source, because it aligns distributions, not points.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect strong alignment when the draw is from the same source (near-exact R, subsuming the known norm-matching hole) and moderate alignment on a held-out different-source draw -- predict 40-60 directions at cosine >0.85, giving a smuggled CNN within 3-6 pp of pixel-space error. The failure mode is local minima; the GW initialisation and multiple restarts are what determine success, so restart count should be an ablation axis. Also note the defensive implication: because the cost only uses pairwise distances, whitening, eps floor and PCA truncation change nothing except the metric used, so this attack is equally effective against all four variants.
attacks.runtime_cost: 2000x2000 Sinkhorn x 200 iterations x 20 restarts: ~1-3 s on A100. GW init on 500-point subsamples: ~0.5 s. Offline artifact: 2,000 whitened public images at int8 81 bytes each = 162 KB -- too big for a 20 KB cap, so ship 200 images (16 KB) or ship a compact generative surrogate (a 10-component whitened GMM: 10 means + rank-12 factors ~ 10 KB) and sample from it.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Zs = subsample(selfwhiten(z_all), 2000)
Xs = sample_from_smuggled_gmm(2000)            # or 200 stored int8 images
R  = gw_init(pairwise_dists(Zs), pairwise_dists(Xs))   # invariant-only init
for t in range(200):
    C = cdist(Zs, Xs @ R.T)**2
    P = sinkhorn(C, reg=0.05, iters=50)
    U, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Zs.T @ P @ Xs)
    R = (U @ Vt).T
# keep the restart with the lowest <P, C>; then reconstruct and classify
attacks.how_to_measure: Transport cost of the winning restart versus the cost at R_true (a calibrated success indicator that needs no ground truth, so the attacker can self-verify). Recovery cosines, reconstruction R^2, frozen-CNN error. Ablate restarts (1/5/20), subsample size (500/2000/5000), and same-source versus held-out-source draw -- the held-out result is the decision-relevant number.

attacks.name: Exact sample matching by Q-invariants (norms, Gram spectrum, distance fingerprints)
attacks.mechanism: The release is a point in R^(Nxd)/O(d), and that quotient is coordinatised exactly by the Gram matrix Z Z^T. So every pairwise distance, every norm, and the whole distance-matrix fingerprint of the released cloud are available verbatim. If the draw is a subset of the public 60k, each released row's Mahalanobis norm ||Sigma^{-1/2}(x-mu)|| is a near-unique 81-dimensional summary statistic; a nearest-neighbour lookup on (norm, top-k distances to a fixed set of anchors) identifies the source image essentially uniquely, after which the label is read off directly and the accuracy is 100%. Even with only norms, collisions are resolved by a second-stage check on the distances to a handful of already-identified anchors. Note this also breaks the two 'k-truncation' and 'separate whitening' variants: truncation just changes the invariant to the norm within the kept subspace, which the informed attacker can also compute.
attacks.expected_effect: Essentially 0% error on a same-source draw, at a cost of one 10,000 x 60,000 distance computation. Organizer already knows this hole. Its inclusion here matters for two reasons: it sets the ceiling that any hold-out design must beat, and it demonstrates that the invariant channel (as opposed to the frame channel) is untouched by every variant under consideration, so no amount of whitening or truncation can help -- only a genuinely unseen draw can.
attacks.runtime_cost: 10k x 60k x 81 distance matmul = 4.9e10 FLOPs, ~5 ms on A100 in fp16; ~40 s CPU. Offline artifact: 60k whitened images is far past the cap, so the practical version ships 60,000 float16 norms = 120 KB (still too big) -- realistically ship a 16-bit hash table of norms for a subset, or recompute norms from a compact seed. This is the one attack the 20 KB source cap genuinely constrains; the organizer should verify that, not assume it.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
nz = np.linalg.norm(selfwhiten(z_train), axis=1)       # Q-invariant
nx = smuggled_public_norms                             # sorted, 16-bit
idx = np.searchsorted(nx_sorted, nz)                   # candidate matches
# disambiguate collisions with distances to 20 anchor rows
D_z = cdist(z_train[:, :], z_train[anchor_ids])
D_x = cdist(pub[cand], pub[anchor_src])
match = argmin over candidates of ||sort(D_z_i) - sort(D_x_c)||
labels = pub_labels[match]
attacks.how_to_measure: Match accuracy and label accuracy as a function of the smuggled artifact size (how many bits of norm per public image are needed). Then repeat on the planned hold-out draw to confirm it drops to chance, which is the number that justifies the hold-out.

attacks.name: Variance-floor tail-subspace anchor (the eps leak, quantified)
attacks.mechanism: With eps > 0 the released covariance is Q diag(lambda/(lambda+eps)) Q^T, not the identity, so second-order statistics are no longer a constant and they identify the low-variance subspace. whiten.py reports 17 pool eigenvalues below 1e-4 and a minimum of 1.5e-8; at eps = 1e-3 those directions have released variance below 0.1 while the bulk sits at ~0.99, a gap of an order of magnitude that is trivially detectable with 20k samples (sampling error on each released eigenvalue is ~sqrt(2/N) ~ 1.4%). The informed attacker knows the corresponding pixel-space subspace (the blank-frame directions), which gives him a 17-dimensional subspace correspondence, and the distinct values lambda_i/(lambda_i+eps) within the tail order the directions individually, pinning R on most of those 17 dimensions rather than just the subspace. The blind attacker gets less but still learns which 17-dimensional subspace is 'dead', which tells him where the border is and combines with the nonnegativity attack. The clean fix is eps = 0 with rank-k truncation, which whiten.py already identifies as the cleanest construction.
attacks.expected_effect: Partial but reliable: expect ~17 directions recovered (as a subspace for sure, individually where lambda_i/(lambda_i+eps) values are separated by more than 1.4%). These are exactly the least useful directions for classification, so standalone smuggling gain is near zero -- but as an initialiser plus a hard constraint on R it reduces attack #5's search space from O(81) to O(64), and it also reveals which released coordinates the honest learner can ignore. Confidence is high that the leak is measurable, lower that it materially improves end-to-end smuggling, which is why both numbers should be reported separately.
attacks.runtime_cost: One eigh: <1 ms. Offline artifact: the 17 bottom pixel-space eigenvectors, 81x17 int8 = 1.4 KB.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
d, V = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(z, rowvar=False))
tail = d < 0.5                                  # ~17 true at eps=1e-3
Vz_t = V[:, tail]
Vx_t = smuggled_bottom_eigvecs                  # 81x17, 1.4 KB
# match within the tail by the predicted variance lam/(lam+eps)
order = np.argsort(d[tail]); order_x = np.argsort(lam_pub[:17]/(lam_pub[:17]+eps))
R_tail = Vz_t[:, order] @ Vx_t[:, order_x].T
# constrain attack #5 to agree with R_tail on span(Vz_t)
attacks.how_to_measure: Report the released-eigenvalue histogram (bimodality of lambda/(lambda+eps)) for eps in {0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2}; number of tail directions individually resolved versus the 1.4% sampling floor; and the delta in attack #5's success rate and end-to-end CNN error with and without the tail constraint. Compare directly against the eps = 0, k = 64 truncated release.

attacks.name: Nonnegativity / zero-atom projection pursuit (blind cone recovery)
attacks.mechanism: This is the blind attack I expect to be strongest, and it is not in the current experiment plan. Pixels satisfy x_p >= 0 with a large atom at exactly zero for the border cells (9x9 area-resize averages ~9.7 raw pixels, so any cell whose support is entirely background is exactly 0). Under any invertible linear release map, 'x_p = 0' becomes 'a_p . z = -mu_p', i.e. a large set of released points lying exactly on a hyperplane; and 'x_p >= 0' becomes a half-space, so the whole released cloud lives in a simplicial cone with 81 facets. Facet directions are therefore recoverable by projection pursuit with a one-sided index: search for unit w maximising the mass of {z_i : w.z_i within h of min_i w.z_i}, i.e. the atom at the lower truncation point.
