Because this exploits an ORDER structure (positivity) rather than a moment, it is the constraint that a Haar rotation is worst at hiding, and it is unaffected by whitening, by the eps floor and by which W was used -- though with whitening the search is over GL(81) rather than O(81), which is the main difficulty. Plumbley's nonnegative-ICA result is the formal version: for well-grounded nonnegative sources the rotation is identifiable from second-order statistics plus nonnegativity alone, with no non-Gaussianity assumption.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect the ~20-30 pixels with substantial exact-zero mass (the frame and near-frame cells) to be recovered well, and the dense interior pixels poorly, because interior cells are rarely exactly zero. That is a partial and somewhat perverse result -- the recovered coordinates are the least informative -- but it anchors the coordinate system enough that topology.recover_layout, run on the recovered facet coordinates, may place the whole lattice. Marked medium-low because the interior recovery is the uncertain part. Two concrete defensive consequences if it lands: (a) a tiny post-whitening dither, z = Q(W(x-mu) + sigma*xi) with sigma ~ 0.02-0.05, destroys the exact-zero atoms at negligible honest cost, and (b) rank-k truncation also destroys them, because zeros are no longer exactly representable in the kept subspace.
attacks.runtime_cost: 20k x 81 projections x 2000 gradient steps: ~200 ms on A100 for all 81 directions in parallel; ~30 s CPU. No offline artifact (blind).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Z = selfwhiten(np.concatenate([z_train, z_test]))
W = orth(np.random.randn(81, 81))
for it in range(2000):
    P = Z @ W                                  # N x 81 projections
    t = np.quantile(P, 0.01, axis=0)           # soft lower edge
    J = np.exp(-((P - t)**2) / h**2).mean(0)   # atom mass near the floor
    G = grad(J.sum(), W)
    W = polar(W + lr * G)                      # keep directions spread out
# also try the GL version: minimise mean(relu(-(Z @ B))**2) + sparsity(Z @ B)
sources = Z @ W; layout = topology.recover_layout(sources**2)
attacks.how_to_measure: First measure the premise: the per-pixel fraction of exactly-zero values in 9x9 area-resized MNIST (predicted: >50% for ~20 border cells, <5% for interior). Then measure recovered-direction cosine against true pixel directions, broken out by that zero fraction. Then adjacency precision and frozen-CNN error. Then re-run with dither sigma in {0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1} to price the countermeasure against honest-learner accuracy.

attacks.name: Blind FastICA (logcosh) -> topology -> CNN, as currently configured
attacks.mechanism: This is the existing attack_ica.py pipeline, and I expect it to FAIL as configured, for three independent reasons worth separating in the write-up. (1) Contrast mismatch: logcosh is the contrast for symmetric super-Gaussian sources; 9x9 MNIST pixels are one-sided and zero-inflated, so the right index is skewness (cube) or a nonnegativity index -- the module's own docstring argues from right-skewness but then defaults to logcosh. (2) Target mismatch: the maximally-independent basis of whitened natural-image-like data is a set of localised oriented filters, not the delta-pixel basis; the module's own zca control acknowledges this, and it means the peak-energy metric has a ceiling well below 1. (3) A structural problem with the hand-off: any basis obtained by rotating whitened data has EXACTLY identity precision, so its partial-correlation matrix is zero and topology.recover_layout has nothing to work with; the pipeline's rescaling by mixing-column norms only restores lattice-shaped partial correlations if ICA already found the pixel basis, which is the thing being tested. Sample size is also marginal: the classical rule N >~ 5 d^2 = 33,000 against 20,000 available rows.
attacks.expected_effect: Predict mean peak-energy fraction in the 0.05-0.25 range against a uniform reference of 0.0123 and a ZCA ceiling I would guess at 0.3-0.5; peak assignment not a bijection; recover_layout either failing or returning a layout whose adjacency precision is near the 0.05 chance level; end-to-end CNN error far above the honest MLP baseline. Report it as the measured negative result that motivates the stronger blind attacks (#11, #13), not as evidence the defence works -- a blind ICA failure says nothing about the informed attacks, which are the ones that decide the design.

attacks.name: Blind skew-based ICA with correct scale restoration
attacks.mechanism: The repaired version of #12. Use the cube (skewness) contrast, which is the matched index for one-sided zero-inflated sources, and fix each source's sign by its third moment (attack_ica.py already does the sign fix). Then, instead of relying on the mixing-column-norm rescaling to recreate lattice-shaped partial correlations, feed topology a statistic that does not require the correct scale: use the matrix of pairwise mutual information or of the correlations of the SQUARED sources (the 'energy correlations' that survive ICA precisely because ICA only removes linear dependence), which for image-like data remain strongly local and are scale-invariant per coordinate. That sidesteps the identity-precision problem entirely: energy correlations of ICA components of images are the classic residual dependency and they are spatially organised.
attacks.expected_effect: Better than #12 but still likely short of pixel recovery. Predict peak-energy fraction ~0.15-0.35 and, more importantly, an energy-correlation matrix whose k-NN graph recovers a 2-D layout with adjacency precision in the 0.3-0.7 range -- enough for the 'locality without identity' threat (#14) but probably not enough to apply a frozen offline CNN, because a frozen CNN needs alignment up to a dihedral, not merely a neighbourhood structure. Include because if it lands even partially it changes the defence conclusion: it is fully blind and therefore survives any hold-out draw.
attacks.runtime_cost: FastICA cube at d=81, N=20k: ~1 s GPU / 30 s CPU. Energy-correlation matrix: <1 ms. Layout search: 12-65 s CPU as measured in topology.py. Blind, no artifact.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
S, Wun, _ = run_ica(unlabeled, fun='cube')          # skewness contrast
S = S * np.sign(((S - S.mean(0))**3).mean(0))       # already in attack_ica
E = np.corrcoef((S**2).T)                           # energy correlations
np.fill_diagonal(E, 0)
layout = topology.recover_layout_from_similarity(E) # bypass partial-corr front end
# compare against topology.recover_layout(positive_part_features(S*scale))
attacks.how_to_measure: Adjacency precision of the layout recovered from energy correlations versus from the current partial-correlation front end, both against ground truth (not against ICA's own peak assignment -- see the note in defence_notes). Report in-competition CNN error trained on the recovered layout (the T1 threat) separately from frozen-offline-CNN error on reconstructed pixels (the T2 threat).

attacks.name: Locality without identity (the threat the metrics may miss)
attacks.mechanism: There are two distinct threats and the current metrics conflate them. T2 is smuggling: apply a frozen offline CNN, which needs the pixel basis recovered up to a dihedral. T1 is weaker and far easier: recover ANY invertible map under which the coordinates have a usable 2-D neighbourhood structure, then train a convolutional learner in-competition. T1 needs no offline artifact, no public data, and no exact alignment -- only that the recovered basis be localised enough for weight sharing to be a good prior. A blind attacker can therefore succeed at T1 while every localisation metric in attack_ica.py (peak energy fraction, bijection, exact placement) reports failure, because those metrics all measure alignment to the true pixel index. If the organizer's goal is only 'stop precomputed features', T1 is arguably legitimate and T2 is the thing to block; if the goal is also 'keep the task permutation-invariant', T1 matters too. Either way the experiment must report them separately, and the decisive quantity is the accuracy GAP between a conv learner on the recovered layout and the best dense learner on the raw released features.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect T1 to partially succeed against every variant via #13's energy correlations, and expect the honest-learner gap to be the thing that decides whether it matters. At 10,000 training examples on 9x9 digits the conv-versus-MLP gap is probably small (my guess: 1-3 pp), in which case T1 is not worth defending against and the whole defence question reduces to T2. That measurement (E4) should be run FIRST, because if the gap is small the entire obfuscation design is optional.
attacks.runtime_cost: No extra cost beyond #13. The decisive baseline (dense MLP on released features) is ~10 s on A100.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
# baseline that decides whether any of this matters:
err_mlp  = fit_predict(z_train, y, z_test, {'family':'mlp'})
err_conv_true = fit_predict(x_train, y, x_test, {'family':'cnn'})   # oracle layout
err_conv_rec  = fit_predict(S_train, y, S_test, {'family':'topo_cnn',
                                                 'layout': layout_from_energy_corr})
# report: (err_mlp - err_conv_true) = the prize;
#         (err_mlp - err_conv_rec)  = what the blind attacker actually wins
attacks.how_to_measure: Run E4 first and report the conv-versus-dense gap on true pixels at n = 10,000, with >=5 seeds and error bars. Then report T1 and T2 as two separate columns for every defence variant. A defence that blocks T2 while leaving T1 open is fine if the gap in the first number is small.

attacks.name: Separate-train/test whitening: free for the attacker, costly for the honest learner
attacks.mechanism: Two sub-cases, both bad. (a) Shared Q, per-split W fitted on each split's own 10,000 rows: the composite mismatch is A_te A_tr^{-1} = Q W_te W_tr^{-1} Q^T = Q (I + E) Q^T where E is the sampling difference of two independent covariance estimates from n = 10,000 in d = 81. Relative spectral error scales as ~sqrt(d/n) = 0.09, so well-conditioned directions shift by ~5-9% and low-variance directions by far more (the eps floor is what keeps this finite). That is a pure covariate shift imposed on the honest learner and worth nothing defensively, because the attacker self-whitens each split independently anyway -- his pipeline is unchanged. Worse, the mismatch matrix is itself anisotropic in the PIXEL basis (its statistics depend on fourth moments of x), so it reintroduces a weak Q-identifying second-order channel between the two splits. (b) Per-split Q: the task becomes unsolvable for an honest learner unless it estimates the relative rotation between splits, which IS the attacker's cumulant-Procrustes attack -- the competition would then reward exactly the capability the organizer is trying to suppress.
attacks.expected_effect: Predict a measurable honest-accuracy loss for separate whitening (my guess: 0.5-3 pp at n = 10,000, larger for linear/MLP learners than for any learner that re-standardises, and largest in the eps-floored tail) and zero attacker cost. Predict that an explicit cross-split alignment step (estimate T = argmin over GL of the discrepancy between the two self-whitened clouds) recovers most of the loss in seconds, confirming the defence is void. Recommendation: one shared map, fitted on the pool, applied identically to train and test. Answer to organizer question (2): joint.
attacks.runtime_cost: Honest-cost measurement: two extra training runs per variant. Attacker's cross-split alignment: one Sinkhorn-Procrustes on 2k x 2k, ~1 s A100.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
# honest cost
for mode in ['joint', 'separate_W', 'separate_Q']:
    ztr, zte = release(mode)
    err[mode] = fit_predict(ztr, y, zte, learner)
# attacker repair of separate_W (should be near-free)
ztr_w, zte_w = selfwhiten(ztr), selfwhiten(zte)
R = sinkhorn_procrustes(zte_w, ztr_w)        # relative rotation, attack #9
err_repaired = fit_predict(ztr_w, y, zte_w @ R.T, learner)
# expect err_repaired ~= err['joint']
attacks.how_to_measure: Honest error for joint / separate-W / separate-Q x {linear, MLP, conv} x >=5 seeds x eps in {0, 1e-3}. Then the attacker-repair number above. Also measure the anisotropy channel: is the spectrum of A_te A_tr^{-1} in the pixel eigenbasis distinguishable from isotropic at n = 10,000 (expect: barely, one draw gives one sample of the fluctuation).

attacks.name: Bootstrap covariance-fluctuation matching (the 8-line fourth-order attack)
attacks.mechanism: A reformulation of the fourth-order channel that is trivial to implement and GPU-friendly. Whitening makes E[Cov_hat(z)] = I, but the FLUCTUATION of the sample covariance around I is not isotropic: Cov(vec(C_hat)) is determined by the fourth moments of x, and it transforms as (R kron R) Cov(vec(C_hat_x)) (R kron R)^T. The attacker bootstraps the released rows to generate B resampled covariance matrices, estimates the covariance of their vectorisations (or, cheaply, a few scalar functionals of it), and matches against the same object computed offline on public MNIST. This is mathematically the same information as the fourth cumulant, but it requires no cumulant algebra -- just resampling and a covariance of covariances -- and it is easy to reduce in dimension (e.g. match only the top eigenvectors of the 6561 x 6561 fluctuation operator, or its trace contraction, which is exactly FOBI). Its value is as an implementation path that a competitor could plausibly write in 20 KB.
attacks.expected_effect: Equivalent in information content to attack #7/#8 and strictly weaker in efficiency (bootstrap noise adds on top of sampling noise), so predict somewhat worse recovery than JADE at the same N -- maybe 30-50 directions at cosine >0.85. Include it because it is the version an attacker is most likely to actually write, and because it makes vivid to the organizer that 'Cov(z) = I exactly' does not mean 'the second-order statistic is a constant': the SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION of that statistic still carries the whole fourth-order channel.
attacks.runtime_cost: B = 500 bootstrap covariances of 81x81 from 20k rows: 500 x (20k x 81 x 81) = 6.6e10 FLOPs, ~10 ms A100 fp16, ~60 s CPU. Offline artifact: top-32 eigenvectors of the 6561-dim fluctuation operator, 6561x32 int8 = 210 KB -- too big, so use the trace-contracted (FOBI) form, 6.7 KB.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Z = selfwhiten(np.concatenate([z_train, z_test]))
Cs = []
for b in range(500):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(Z), len(Z))
    Cs.append(np.cov(Z[idx], rowvar=False).ravel())
F = np.cov(np.array(Cs), rowvar=False)           # 6561 x 6561 (or contract)
Kz = F.reshape(81,81,81,81).trace(axis1=1, axis2=3)   # -> FOBI-like 81x81
d, V = np.linalg.eigh(Kz); R = (V * signs) @ smuggled_Vx.T
attacks.how_to_measure: Compare directly against attack #7 (analytic FOBI) at the same N: the bootstrap version should match it up to bootstrap noise, which validates the equivalence claim. Report recovery cosines and the number of bootstrap replicates needed before the estimate stabilises.

attacks.name: Lattice-prior (DCT) eigenvector matching
attacks.mechanism: A blind attacker cannot recover an element of O(81) from a rotation-invariant prior -- Haar Q is a perfect one-time pad on the frame. Every blind attack therefore smuggles in a non-rotation-invariant prior, and the weakest such prior is 'it is a smooth image on a 9x9 lattice'. Under that prior the pixel covariance is approximately that of a stationary GMRF on a lattice, whose eigenvectors are approximately the separable 2-D DCT basis, ordered by spatial frequency. So the blind attacker eigendecomposes C_z = Q Sigma Q^T, matches eigenvector j to DCT basis function j by eigenvalue rank, and reads off Q_hat = V_z D_dct^T. The related and stronger form is a sparse-precision search: a lattice GMRF has a precision matrix with ~4 non-zeros per row, so minimise ||R^T C_z^{-1} R||_1 over O(81) by Givens sweeps initialised from the DCT match. Both die completely under whitening, since the precision becomes exactly I -- which is the cleanest statement of what whitening buys against a blind attacker.
attacks.expected_effect: Expect partial success on the lowest few frequencies and rapid degradation, because MNIST's 9x9 covariance is strongly non-stationary (the border is dead and the centre of mass is off-centre), so its eigenvectors are not DCT functions beyond the first handful; and the eigenvalue rank ordering of the true Sigma does not match the DCT frequency ordering in the tail. Predict reconstruction R^2 ~0.3-0.6 and an offline-CNN error far above pixel-space. The sparse-precision variant should do substantially better -- I would guess adjacency precision 0.5-0.8 -- because it uses the lattice structure directly rather than through a stationarity assumption. Marked low-medium for the DCT form; the point of running it is to establish that rotation-only is broken even for a blind attacker, which strengthens the case for whitening independently of attack #1.
attacks.runtime_cost: DCT form: one eigh, <1 ms. Sparse-precision Givens search: 3240 pairs x 50 sweeps on an 81x81 matrix, ~1-5 s CPU, ~50 ms A100. Blind, no artifact.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
d, V = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(z, rowvar=False))       # descending after flip
D = dct2_basis(9)                                    # 81x81, freq-ordered
R0 = V[:, ::-1] @ D.T
# stronger: sparse-precision refinement
P = np.linalg.inv(np.cov(z, rowvar=False) + 1e-4*np.eye(81))
R = R0
for sweep in range(50):
    for (i, j) in all_pairs:
        theta = argmin_theta l1norm(givens(i,j,theta).T @ (R.T @ P @ R) @ givens(...))
        R = R @ givens(i, j, theta)
layout = topology.recover_layout_from_precision(R.T @ P @ R)
attacks.how_to_measure: Reconstruction R^2 and adjacency precision for both forms, against the whiten+rotate release as the control (where both must collapse to chance -- that collapse is the measurement that answers 'does whitening help at all against a blind attacker'). Also report the L1 norm of the recovered precision against the L1 norm of the true pixel precision as a self-verifiable success indicator.

red:linear-algebra.defence_notes:
DOMINANCE RANKING (the short answer to the three questions).

(1) Is rotation alone enough? No, and the reason is one eigendecomposition. Rotation-only releases Cov(z) = Q Sigma Q^T; an informed attacker matches eigenvectors against public 9x9 MNIST's Sigma and fixes the 81 sign bits with per-direction skewness comparisons (attack #3). Whitening is therefore NECESSARY. But the self-whitening lemma (attack #1) shows it is far from sufficient: the attacker whitens the released cloud himself, at which point rotation-only, ZCA+eps, PCA+eps and rank-k truncation all become the SAME problem -- estimate one unknown element of O(81). Whitening deletes exactly the 3321 equations of the unconditional covariance out of roughly 1.9M identifying equations available to an informed attacker (class means 810, class-conditional covariances 33,210, third cumulants ~88k, fourth ~1.8M). That is ~0.2% of his constraints. It removes the cheapest and most robust channel, which is worth doing, and nothing else.

(2) Separate or joint whitening? Joint, unambiguously. Separate-W is strictly dominated: it imposes a covariate shift on honest learners of order sqrt(d/n) = sqrt(81/10000) ~ 9% relative in the covariance, while costing the attacker nothing (he self-whitens each split independently regardless) and weakly reintroducing a Q-identifying channel through the anisotropy of the cross-split mismatch. Separate-Q is worse than dominated: it makes the honest task solvable only by performing the attacker's own cross-split rotation-alignment, i.e. it turns the competition into a rotation-recovery contest.

(3) Can an attacker still get the pixel basis? Against an INFORMED attacker, I expect yes, via attack #5 (class-conditional covariance Procrustes) -- 10 class covariances give 33,210 equations for 3240 unknowns, degeneracy-proof, second-order only so it does not need non-Gaussianity, ~20 ms on an A100, and a ~10 KB rank-truncated artifact. Attack #8 (JADE cumulant Procrustes) is the label-free equivalent and is the one that matters most for the hold-out draw, since it works on distributional similarity rather than sample identity. Against a BLIND attacker I expect whiten+rotate to hold for pixel-exact recovery (attack #12 should fail as configured), but NOT necessarily for the weaker "locality without identity" threat (#14).

THE ISSUE THAT OVERRIDES EVERYTHING ELSE. whiten.py's docstring says the transform is fitted on the whole 60,000-image pool and "must be published with the protocol". If (mu, W, Q) are a published or fixed constant, none of these attacks are needed: the attacker folds A_inv into the first layer of an offline CNN, or ships A_inv itself as 81x81 int8 = 6,723 bytes inside a 20 KB cap (attack #2). That is the same shape of failure as the measured 1.8 KB unpermute table. The defence is only meaningful if (mu, W, Q) are freshly drawn per submission from a secret seed, which also means the attacker's work must fit in the scored runtime -- and that is where the real security margin lives, not in the algebra. Resolve this before running E1-E4.

VARIANT RECOMMENDATIONS.
- ZCA vs PCA is a no-op. whiten.py already proves it: Q W_zca = (QU) W_pca with QU Haar. E3 as scoped will measure float noise. Drop that axis and spend the budget on eps vs k.
- eps floor leaks. Cov(z) = Q diag(lam/(lam+eps)) Q^T is not the identity; with eps = 1e-3 the 17 pool eigenvalues below 1e-4 sit at released variance <0.1 against a bulk of ~0.99, a gap ~70x the 1.4% sampling floor at N = 20k. That hands over a 17-dimensional subspace correspondence plus, where lam/(lam+eps) values are separated by more than 1.4%, the individual directions within it. Prefer eps = 0 with rank-k truncation (k ~ 64), which whiten.py already identifies as the cleanest construction: exactly identity covariance, no tail to leak, no 8000x noise amplification.
- Rank-k truncation buys almost nothing beyond removing the eps leak: the informed attacker knows which top-k eigenspace was kept. Its one genuine side benefit is that it destroys the exact-zero structure that attack #11 depends on.
- Consider a small post-whitening dither, z = Q(W(x-mu) + sigma*xi) with sigma ~ 0.02-0.05. It adds no rotational security (isotropic noise is Q-equivariant) but it destroys the exact-zero hyperplane atoms that the nonnegativity attack exploits, and it caps the precision of every moment-matching attack. Price it against honest accuracy.

TWO METHODOLOGY PROBLEMS IN THE EXISTING ATTACK HARNESS (mnist/experiments/pmnist-medium-cutoffs-20260923/attack_ica.py).
(a) The adjacency metrics are self-referential. `adjacency_precision` and `exact_placement_fraction_best_dihedral` are computed against `true_adjacent`, which is built from `report["peak_pixel"]` -- ICA's own peak assignment -- not from the ground-truth pixel index. If ICA fails to localise, those metrics compare a recovered layout against a garbage reference and can look arbitrarily good or bad for reasons unrelated to correctness. Only `cnn_query_error_pct` currently measures the attack end to end. Add a ground-truth-anchored adjacency precision.
(b) `positive_part_features` squares the range-normalised sources so topology's sqrt front end sees an affine map of them. That part is right, but it also flattens the per-feature variance scale, so topology's variance screen (ACTIVE_VARIANCE = 1e-5) will screen out nothing -- on real pixels it removes 15-18 dead cells. The layout search therefore runs in a different regime than the one it was validated in. Either rescale to pixel-like variances or disable the screen explicitly and say so.
(c) The default contrast is logcosh, which targets symmetric super-Gaussian sources; the module's own motivation argues from right-skewness. Measure `cube` too, and the nonnegativity index of attack #11. As configured, a null result from E1 would be weak evidence.

RUN E4 FIRST. The quantity that decides whether any of this matters is the honest conv-versus-dense accuracy gap on true pixels at n = 10,000 on 9x9 digits. If that gap is 1-2 pp, the spatial prior is worth almost nothing, smuggling buys almost nothing, and the entire obfuscation layer can be dropped in favour of the two defences already known to work: a genuinely held-out draw (which is the only thing that closes the Q-invariant sample-matching channel, since pairwise distances survive every variant) plus the source-size cap. Two threats should be scored in separate columns throughout: T1 = recover any locally-structured basis and train a conv net in-competition (easy, arguably legitimate); T2 = recover pixels up to a dihedral and apply frozen offline weights (hard, the actual thing to block). Every localisation metric in the current harness measures T2 only.

attacks.name: Non-negative orthant facet recovery (min-projection / Plumbley NNICA)
attacks.mechanism: Images are non-negative and every 9x9 area-resized pixel is EXACTLY zero in a large fraction of images (measured on the pool: min zero-fraction over all 81 pixels = 4.36%, 48/81 pixels are zero in >50% of images, 79/81 in >5%). Let a_p be row p of A^{-1}; then a_p.z = x_p - mu_p >= -mu_p with equality on every sample whose pixel p is zero. So each pixel is a SUPPORTING FACET of the released point cloud, touched by >=870 of 20,000 samples. Define the scale-invariant contrast g(w) = (mean_i w.z_i - min_i w.z_i)/std_i(w.z_i). I measured g on the whitened pool: all 81 pixel directions have g <= 1.67 (most < 0.8), while 2000 random directions in the same whitened space have g in [3.22, 9], 1st percentile 3.73. That is a hard, gap-free separation -- every pixel direction is an extreme outlier of a statistic computable with no side information. Plumbley's non-negative-ICA theorem makes this exact rather than heuristic: for non-negative, 'well-grounded' sources (density touching 0), the orthogonal rotation of whitened data that renders all reconstructed coordinates non-negative is unique up to permutation and scale -- source INDEPENDENCE is not required, which matters because MNIST pixels are strongly dependent and hence a bad fit for ordinary ICA. The attack is affine-equivariant: it searches all of GL(81) via the ratio objective, so it works identically against rotation-only, ZCA+rotate, eps-floored, and (to within the discarded variance, <1e-4 per direction vs sigma_p ~ 0.1-0.3) PCA-truncated releases.
attacks.expected_effect: Recovers the pixel basis up to permutation and positive scale. With 20k rows (10k train + 10k transductive test) and 81 dims the facets are supported by 870-19,900 samples each, so the LP/soft-min estimate of each a_p is determined to ~1/sqrt(870) ~ 3% relative -- far tighter than needed. Expect 60-81 of 81 pixel directions with matched energy >0.9; the weakest are the four corners (variance 1.5e-8) which carry no information anyway. Once the basis is permutation-recovered, the already-measured 1.8 KB Hungarian table (tmp/unpermute-demo) undoes the permutation in 17 ms CPU at 67-71/81 pixels correct, and topology.recover_layout gives the 9x9 lattice from the recovered pixels. End-to-end this hands the attacker the raw pixel problem, i.e. the entire defence is void.
attacks.runtime_cost: GPU soft-min variant: 81x81 unknowns, 2000 Adam steps on a 20000x81 batch = ~5e11 FLOPs, ~0.5-3 s on an A100 (launch-bound, not FLOP-bound); can be cut to ~200 ms with fused steps and 500 restarts batched. Exact LP variant (maximise ties subject to w.z_i + c >= 0), 81 LPs x 20k constraints x 82 vars: ~30-120 s CPU, so the GPU variant is what a scored submission would ship. Offline artifact: ZERO bytes -- the attack is fully blind. Only the downstream permutation table (1.8 KB) and a pixel-space classifier (0.8-15 KB) need smuggling, comfortably inside 20 KB.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Z = torch.cat([train_x, test_x])                    # (20000, 81), transductive
Z = (Z - Z.mean(0)) / Z.std(0)                       # conditioning only
M = torch.randn(R, 81, 81, device='cuda', requires_grad=True)   # R=512 restarts x 81 rows
opt = torch.optim.Adam([M], 3e-2)
for step in range(2000):
    P = torch.einsum('rpd,nd->rpn', M / M.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True), Z)
    soft_min = -(torch.logsumexp(-P / tau, dim=-1) * tau)        # tau ~ 0.02 * P.std()
    g = (P.mean(-1) - soft_min) / P.std(-1)                      # (R, 81) contrast
    rep = repulsion(M)                                           # keep rows distinct: sum of |cos| off-diag
    (g.mean() + 0.1 * rep).backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
# collect all rows over all restarts with g < 2.5, cluster by |cosine| > 0.98,
# keep the 81 largest clusters -> Ahat_inv (81,81); pixels = Z @ Ahat_inv.T + offset
# offset_p = -min_i (Ahat_inv[p] . z_i)
# then: est = hungarian(match(pixel means/stds, smuggled 162 B table)); apply smuggled CNN
attacks.how_to_measure: (a) Histogram g(w) for the 81 true pixel directions vs 10^4 random directions in each released variant -- confirm the 1.67 vs 3.22 separation survives eps-floor and PCA truncation. (b) Hungarian matched-energy between recovered rows of Ahat_inv and true rows of A^{-1}, restricted to the 64 pixels with variance > 1e-4; report fraction with matched energy > 0.9. (c) Feed recovered pixels to topology.recover_layout and report adjacency precision and exact_placement_fraction_best_dihedral. (d) End-to-end: apply an offline-trained pixel-space CNN to the recovered pixels and report query error % vs the honest MLP baseline, and the wall-clock/joules of the recovery step.

attacks.name: Frozen offline network plus learned linear adapter (no basis recovery at all)
attacks.mechanism: This is the structural reason no invertible linear release can work. The organizer's known fact 'any linear model is exactly invariant to an invertible linear release map' generalises: for ANY frozen nonlinear f trained offline in pixel space, the composite class {f(Mz + b) : M in GL(81), b in R^81} contains f(x) exactly, because M = A^{-1}, b = mu is in the class. So a smuggled pretrained CNN loses NOTHING in expressive power under any of the four variants -- the release only imposes the cost of estimating 6561 (or 6642 with the offset) extra parameters from the 10k labelled rows. If the attacker also knows W (published protocol, pool-derived, see attack 'Known-whitener norm matching'), the adapter can be constrained to M = W^{-1}Q^T with Q on the Stiefel manifold, cutting the free parameters to 3240 and making the fit essentially noiseless. The attacker never needs to know which coordinate is which pixel; they just need the composition to work.
attacks.expected_effect: 10,000 labelled samples for 6561 linear parameters feeding a frozen feature extractor is a comfortable regime (roughly 1.5 samples/parameter, but the effective capacity is far lower because the frozen net's Jacobian is low-rank and the adapter can be regularised toward orthogonality using the known W). Expect the smuggled path to land within ~0.2-0.5 percentage points of the offline CNN's pixel-space error on the same 10k train rows, i.e. to clear the 2-3% bands that an honest from-scratch learner on 10k obfuscated rows would struggle to reach. Adding a transductive entropy / consistency loss on the 10k unlabelled test rows tightens it further. The Stiefel-constrained version should be strictly better and is the one to measure.
attacks.runtime_cost: In-submission: 20-60 epochs of adapter-only training over 10k x 81 through a ~15k-parameter 9x9 CNN = well under 1e12 FLOPs, ~1-3 s and a few hundred joules on an A100. Offline artifact: the CNN itself. At int8 with per-tensor scales a 15k-parameter 9x9 CNN is ~15 KB raw; base64 inside a 20 KB source cap forces ~11 KB binary, i.e. ~11k int8 params or ~22k int4 params. That is still a serious 9x9 model. The 1.8 KB softmax-regression artifact already measured gives 87% for free as a fallback.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
W = whitening_from_published_protocol()      # attacker recomputes from public pool
net = load_int8_cnn(SMUGGLED_BLOB)            # frozen, trained offline on public 9x9 MNIST
Q = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.eye(81, device='cuda'))
opt = torch.optim.Adam([Q], 1e-3)
for ep in range(40):
    for zb, yb in batches(train_z, train_y):
        Qo, _ = torch.linalg.qr(Q)            # or Cayley / expm parameterisation
        xb = (zb @ Qo) @ torch.linalg.inv(W).T + mu     # 3240 free params, not 6561
        loss = F.cross_entropy(net(xb.view(-1,1,9,9)), yb)
        loss = loss + 0.1 * relu(-xb).pow(2).mean()     # non-negativity prior: free extra signal
        loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
# fallback if validation on held-out train rows is poor: run the honest learner instead
attacks.how_to_measure: Train the frozen CNN offline on public 9x9 MNIST (excluding the draw if a hold-out draw is used), then fit (i) an unconstrained 81x81 adapter and (ii) a Stiefel-constrained adapter on 10k released rows, for each of the four variants. Report query error % against three baselines: the same CNN on true pixels, the honest MLP on released features, and the honest topo_cnn. Also report joules/seconds of the adapter fit so the organizer can see whether the defence prices the attack out (it does not). Sweep n in {1000, 3162, 10000} -- the interesting question is at what n the 6561 extra parameters actually start to hurt.

attacks.name: Known-whitener norm matching plus orthogonal Procrustes (exact-source draw)
attacks.mechanism: whiten.py fits W and mu on the 60,000-image public MNIST pool and the protocol publishes method and epsilon. Therefore the attacker can RECOMPUTE W and mu exactly; only Q is secret. Set y_i = W(x_i - mu) for public image i -- fully computable offline. The release is z = Q y, and Q is orthogonal, so ||z|| = ||y|| is an EXACT per-sample invariant. Match released rows to public images by norm (and disambiguate ties by a second invariant such as ||z||_4 or the nearest-neighbour distance profile, since all pairwise distances are preserved too). A handful of matched pairs then gives Q in closed form by orthogonal Procrustes: Q = UV^T from the SVD of Z_matched^T Y_matched. 81 correct matches suffice; 200 makes it numerically exact. This completely defeats whitening -- whitening is attacker-reproducible, so it hides nothing.
attacks.expected_effect: Exact recovery of Q, hence exact recovery of every pixel, hence the attacker can simply read the TEST LABELS off the matched public images (0% error) or, more discreetly, apply an offline pixel-space CNN. Norm collision analysis: ||W(x-mu)|| ranges over roughly [5, 14] across the pool with 60,000 candidates, so the typical sorted gap is ~1.5e-4, while float32 release preserves the norm to ~1e-6 relative (~1e-5 absolute). Matching is therefore essentially unique; even 1% correct matches (200 rows) is more than enough for Procrustes. Crucially, PARTIAL overlap is fatal: if only 0.1% of the draw comes from the public set, Q is still fully recovered and all 20,000 rows are then in pixel space. This is why a hold-out draw must have literally zero overlap with anything derivable from public 9x9 data.
attacks.runtime_cost: In-submission: norms of 20k x 81 (~3 MFLOP), a sorted merge against a smuggled norm table, one 81x81 SVD. Under 10 ms on an A100. Offline artifact is the binding constraint: 60,000 float16 norms = 120 KB, over the 20 KB cap. Workarounds that fit: (a) smuggle only ~500 public images' norms quantised to uint16 (1 KB) plus those 500 images at int4 (~20 KB, tight) -- but a specific public image appears in a 20k-of-60k draw only w.p. 1/3, so ~170 of 500 land, still plenty for Procrustes; (b) better, smuggle nothing and bootstrap Q from the 810-byte class-mean table (see 'Class-mean subspace equations') plus non-negativity; (c) if the scored container has network access or a copy of MNIST on disk, the artifact cost is zero -- check this.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
W, mu = recompute_from_public_pool(method='zca', eps=1e-3)   # protocol is published
norm_tab, img_tab = SMUGGLED            # (500,) uint16 norms, (500,81) int4 pixels
zn = np.linalg.norm(train_z, axis=1)                          # (10000,)
yn = norm_tab.astype(np.float64) * NORM_SCALE
j = np.abs(zn[:, None] - yn[None, :]).argmin(1)
ok = np.abs(zn - yn[j]) < 1e-4                                # ~170 hits expected
Y = (img_tab[j[ok]] / 15.0 - mu) @ W.T                        # (m, 81)
U, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(train_z[ok].T @ Y)
Q = U @ Vt                                   # z = Q y  =>  x = W^{-1} Q^T z + mu
X_test = test_z @ Q @ np.linalg.inv(W).T + mu
pred = smuggled_cnn(X_test)
attacks.how_to_measure: On an exact-source draw: report ||Qhat - Q||_F, the number of norm matches that are correct, and the resulting test error (expect ~0%). Then repeat with an artificially reduced overlap (1%, 0.1%, 0.01% of the draw drawn from the public set) to find the overlap threshold at which Procrustes stops recovering Q -- this number tells the organizer exactly how clean the hold-out draw must be. Also verify the corollary: that publishing the protocol (method + eps + pool) is what makes W attacker-computable, by re-running with W fitted on a secret pool the attacker does not have.

attacks.name: Amortised offline crack, then smuggle the 81x81 inverse (fixed Q across draws)
attacks.mechanism: whiten.py uses a single fixed DEFAULT_ROTATION_SEED = 20260923 and fits W on the fixed 60k pool, so A is a CONSTANT across all draws, seeds and submissions. Any attacker who cracks A once -- offline, with unlimited compute, on any released draw (a dev/practice draw, a public leaderboard sample, their own submission's inputs exfiltrated through the score channel) -- can then hard-code A^{-1} and skip the in-submission recovery entirely. The 20 KB source cap does not stop this: 81x81 float16 = 13.1 KB (17.5 KB base64, fits); 81x81 int8 with 81 per-row float16 scales = 6.72 KB (9.0 KB base64, comfortable); and int8 is far more precision than needed because the downstream CNN is robust to a ~0.4% relative error in the adapter. This collapses every one of the four variants to a no-op regardless of how expensive the original crack was.
attacks.expected_effect: Complete and free defeat. Even if the strongest attack cost 100 GPU-hours offline, it is paid once. The in-submission cost drops to one 20000x81 by 81x81 matmul. A defence whose secret is a constant across the whole competition has an effective security level of 'one determined entrant, once'. Note this also converts every attack below from an in-submission-budget question into an offline question, so runtime-cost arguments for the defence evaporate.
attacks.runtime_cost: In-submission: one GEMM, ~0.26 GFLOP, <1 ms on an A100. Offline artifact 6.7-13.1 KB (plus the classifier, so the real budget is ~6.7 KB matrix + ~11 KB int8 CNN = 17.7 KB binary, which base64 overruns; in practice the attacker ships the 6.7 KB matrix + the 1.8 KB linear model for the 8-12% bands, or drops to int4 weights for the CNN).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
# ---- offline, once ----
# crack A by any attack in this list on any released draw, then
Ainv = np.linalg.inv(A_hat)                           # (81, 81)
scale = np.abs(Ainv).max(1) / 127
blob = base64.b85encode(zlib.compress(
    np.round(Ainv / scale[:, None]).astype(np.int8).tobytes()
    + scale.astype(np.float16).tobytes()))            # ~9 KB of source
# ---- in submission ----
Ainv = decode(blob)
X_tr = train_z @ Ainv.T + MU; X_te = test_z @ Ainv.T + MU
pred = smuggled_cnn(X_te)      # or: finetune the smuggled CNN on (X_tr, train_y)
attacks.how_to_measure: Quantise the true A^{-1} to int8 per row and float16, apply to a fresh draw, and report (i) reconstruction PSNR against true pixels, (ii) the offline CNN's query error under each quantisation, (iii) the exact base64 source size. Then measure the same with a FRESH Q per draw and confirm the smuggled matrix becomes useless (error ~90%), so the organizer can see that per-evaluation Q re-randomisation is the cheap fix -- and separately measure how much of the crack survives per-evaluation Q (only the 3240 Q parameters must be re-solved in-submission, since W and mu stay constant).

attacks.name: Epsilon-floor tail leak: corner-pixel axes from the released covariance
attacks.mechanism: With a variance floor the released covariance is Q diag(lambda/(lambda+eps)) Q^T, not the identity, so its eigenvectors ARE identified wherever the shrinkage factors are distinct. I measured the pool spectrum: the six smallest eigenvalues are 1.51e-8, 3.10e-8, 2.11e-7, 3.11e-7, 3.85e-7, 4.07e-7 and their eigenvectors are almost exactly single pixels -- peak energy 0.994, 1.000, 0.999, 0.998, 0.919, 0.915 on pixels (0,0), (8,0), (8,8), (0,8), (0,1), (1,0), with effective support 1.0-1.3. At eps=1e-3 these become released variances 1.51e-5, 3.10e-5, 2.11e-4, 3.11e-4, 3.85e-4, 4.06e-4 -- mutually separated by factors of 2.05, 6.79, 1.48, 1.24, 1.06, and separated from the seventh (1.25e-2) by a factor of 31. Davis-Kahan with n=20,000 gives eigenvector perturbation ~ sqrt(l_i l_j / n)/|l_i - l_j| ~ 0.01 rad for the tightest of these pairs. So the blind attacker reads off, from the released covariance alone in one eigh call, four exact corner-pixel axes plus two edge-adjacent ones, and a further ~11 directions spanning the always-black frame (74/81 directions are shrunk below 0.99 at eps=1e-3; 29 below 0.5). That is a precise anchor: the four corners fix the lattice frame AND resolve the dihedral ambiguity that topology.py says no unlabelled statistic can break, which is exactly the residual the existing pipeline needs.
attacks.expected_effect: Recovers >=4 exact pixel axes and a ~17-dimensional border subspace with essentially no error, blind, from second-order statistics only, in one eigendecomposition. On its own that is 4-6 of 81 pixels, not a win; combined with non-negativity or ICA on the remaining 64-dimensional complement it removes the dihedral ambiguity, seeds the lattice, and shrinks the search from SO(81) (3240 params) to SO(64) (2016 params). At eps=1e-2 the leak is much worse (81/81 directions shrunk below 0.99, 47 below 0.5), so the currently-defaulted attack_ica epsilon of 1e-2 is the most leaky setting in the file. The fix is PCA truncation to k ~ 64: Cov(z) is then exactly I, there is no tail, and this attack returns pure Wishart noise.
attacks.runtime_cost: One 81x81 eigendecomposition of a sample covariance over 20k rows: ~0.3 ms on CPU, negligible on GPU. Offline artifact: 0 bytes (blind). The subsequent dihedral resolution needs the 162-byte mean/std table at most.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Z = np.concatenate([train_z, test_z])               # 20000 x 81
C = np.cov(Z, rowvar=False)
d, V = np.linalg.eigh(C)                           # ascending
# the shrunk tail: directions with d << median(d)
tail = np.where(d < 0.5 * np.median(d))[0]
# V[:, tail[:4]] are (up to sign) Q @ e_corner for the four corners
# sanity: their projections are near-constant and near-minimal
proj = Z @ V[:, tail[:6]]
assert (proj.std(0) / proj.std()).max() < 0.1
# use them to fix orientation, then run the SO(64) attack on the complement
comp = V[:, d > 0.5 * np.median(d)]                # 20000 x ~64 subproblem
attacks.how_to_measure: For eps in {0, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2}: report how many released-covariance eigenvectors have matched energy > 0.9 against a true pixel axis (Hungarian on |V^T A|), and the estimated eigenvector angle error vs the Davis-Kahan prediction at n in {1k, 10k, 20k}. Then report whether supplying those anchors to topology.py / the ICA pipeline improves adjacency precision and end-to-end CNN error relative to running without them. Include the PCA-truncated k=64 release as the control where this must return chance (matched energy ~1/81).

attacks.name: Rotation-only: exact eigen-matching of the released covariance
attacks.mechanism: With W = I the released covariance is exactly Q Sigma Q^T where Sigma is the public pool's pixel covariance. Eigendecompose both: Sigma = U L U^T (known offline), Cov(z) = Vhat Lhat Vhat^T (computed from 20k released rows). Then Q = Vhat U^T up to a sign per eigenvector and up to rotations within degenerate eigen-subspaces; the signs are fixed by any third-order statistic (pixel skewness is strongly positive, as attack_ica already exploits) or by non-negativity of the reconstruction. I measured the relative eigen-gaps of the pool covariance: the top 20 eigenvalues are 0.425, 0.268, 0.232, 0.215, 0.199, 0.152, ... with relative gaps of 37%, 14%, 7.1%, 7.6%, 24%, 21%, 18%, 5.8%, 9.1%, 23%, ... -- only two of the top 20 gaps fall below 3%. Sampling error at n=20,000 is lambda*sqrt(2/n) = 1.0% relative, so Davis-Kahan gives eigenvector errors of roughly 0.015 rad for the top pairs and under 0.2 rad even for the tightest (eigenvalues 17/18, gap 1.8%).
attacks.expected_effect: Essentially exact recovery of Q in closed form for the top ~40 directions, adequate for the rest, from ONE eigendecomposition. There is no meaningful residual ambiguity: 81 distinct eigenvalues means the only freedom is 81 signs, and skewness or non-negativity fixes all of them. Rotation-only is therefore not a defence at all against anyone who has the public pool -- it is strictly weaker than the pixel permutation it replaces, because the permutation at least required a Hungarian match while this is a single matrix product. Expect the smuggled pixel-space CNN to run at full pixel-space accuracy.
attacks.runtime_cost: In-submission: one 81x81 eigendecomposition plus two GEMMs, ~1 ms on an A100. Offline artifact: U and L for the public pool, 81x81 float16 = 13.1 KB (fits, tightly), or better, ship the 81x81 int8 version at 6.7 KB, or recompute nothing and ship only the eigenvalue-ordering plus a coarse int8 U.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
U, L = SMUGGLED_pool_eigh            # from public 60k MNIST at 9x9, int8 + scales
Z = np.concatenate([train_z, test_z])
Lh, Vh = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(Z, rowvar=False))
Q = Vh[:, ::-1] @ U[:, ::-1].T        # match by descending eigenvalue
X = Z @ Q + POOL_MEAN                 # candidate pixels
sgn = np.sign(skew(X, axis=0));       # fix the 81 sign ambiguities
Q = Q * sgn[None, :]; X = Z @ Q + POOL_MEAN
X = np.clip(X, 0, 1)                  # non-negativity as a check: violations ~ 0
pred = smuggled_cnn(X[len(train_z):])
attacks.how_to_measure: Report ||Qhat - Q||_F and the per-eigenvector angle error as a function of n in {1k, 3.2k, 10k, 20k}, against the Davis-Kahan prediction sqrt(l_i l_j/n)/|l_i - l_j|. Report reconstruction PSNR of the recovered pixels and the end-to-end smuggled-CNN query error. This is the control that establishes 'rotation alone is not enough' -- it should be the cleanest, most decisive number in the whole study.

attacks.name: Rotation-only, blind: image-prior (DCT / Markov-lattice) eigenmode matching
attacks.mechanism: Without the public pool the attacker still knows the data are 9x9 non-negative images. The covariance of any approximately stationary lattice field is diagonalised by the 2-D DCT basis, with eigenvalues ordered by spatial frequency; separable first-order Markov models Sigma = R(rho) kron R(rho) give an explicit one-parameter family. So: eigendecompose Cov(z), fit rho by matching the observed eigenvalue profile, and set Qhat = Vhat U_DCT(rho)^T. Ambiguities: 2-D DCT modes (i,j) and (j,i) are exactly degenerate under a symmetric separable model, giving ~36 two-fold ambiguities, and MNIST is not stationary so the true ordering deviates from the model ordering. Both are resolved by a second stage: the non-negativity contrast of attack #1 restricted to small perturbations of Qhat, or simply using Qhat as the initialisation for that optimiser instead of random restarts.
attacks.expected_effect: Alone: a coarse Q with the low-frequency modes right and the mid/high-frequency modes scrambled among near-degenerate groups -- probably enough for a CNN adapter to finetune from, but not exact. As an initialiser for the non-negativity attack it should cut the restart count by an order of magnitude and remove the main failure mode (bad local optima). This is the attack that answers 'is rotation-only safe against someone with no dataset-specific knowledge?' -- I expect the answer to be no, but with genuine uncertainty about how much of the mid-spectrum survives the non-stationarity of digit images.
attacks.runtime_cost: One eigendecomposition plus a 1-D grid search over rho: <10 ms. Offline artifact: 0 bytes -- the DCT basis is generated by 5 lines of code, which is the whole point (it defeats the source cap by construction).
attacks.implementation_sketch:
def dct2_basis(n=9):
    k = np.arange(n); D = np.cos(np.pi * (k[:,None] + 0.5) * k[None,:] / n)
    D /= np.linalg.norm(D, axis=0); return np.kron(D, D)          # 81 x 81
U = dct2_basis()
best = None
for rho in np.linspace(0.5, 0.99, 50):
    R = rho ** np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(9), np.arange(9)))
    lam = np.kron(np.linalg.eigvalsh(R), np.linalg.eigvalsh(R))
    score = spearman(np.sort(lam)[::-1], np.sort(Lh)[::-1])
    best = max(best or (0,None), (score, rho))
order = np.argsort(-model_eigs(best[1]))
Q0 = Vh[:, np.argsort(-Lh)] @ U[:, order].T       # seed for the NN-facet optimiser
attacks.how_to_measure: Matched energy of Qhat^T against true pixel axes; fraction of the 81 DCT modes assigned to the correct frequency pair; and -- the number that matters -- the reduction in restarts/iterations the non-negativity attack needs when seeded with Q0 instead of random, plus whether the seeded run reaches a better optimum. Run on both the exact-source draw and the hold-out 9x9 draw, since this attack uses no dataset-specific information and so should transfer unchanged.

attacks.name: Class-conditional covariance joint diagonalisation
attacks.mechanism: The submission gets 10,000 LABELLED train rows, so it can form 10 class-conditional released covariances Chat_c = A Sigma_c A^T. With W recomputable from the published protocol, the attacker also knows the 10 target matrices T_c = W Sigma_c W^T offline, and the relation is Chat_c = Q T_c Q^T for a single unknown orthogonal Q -- ten simultaneous 81x81 matrix equations for 3240 unknowns, massively overdetermined. Closed-form seed: eigendecompose T_0 and Chat_0 and set Q = Vhat_0 V_0^T, resolving the 81 sign ambiguities and any near-degenerate blocks with a second class; then refine by approximate joint diagonalisation (minimise sum_c ||Q^T Chat_c Q - T_c||_F^2 over the Stiefel manifold). Unlike the marginal covariance, class-conditional covariances are NOT rotation-invariant after whitening, so this breaks the symmetry that whitening was supposed to create. Note that only the labels make this possible -- it is the price of releasing a supervised training set.
attacks.expected_effect: Statistically the sample size is the limiting factor: ~1000 rows per class for an 81x81 covariance means sqrt(81/1000) = 28% relative operator-norm error per class, so individual Chat_c eigenvectors are unreliable in near-degenerate blocks. But there are 10 of them and only 3240 parameters to fit, so the joint estimate should be far better than any single one. My estimate: Q recovered to within 0.05-0.2 rad on the top half of the spectrum, degrading in the tail -- good enough to initialise a CNN adapter, probably not good enough for exact pixel recovery on its own. Against a hold-out draw from a different 9x9 dataset the T_c are only approximately right, which I expect degrades this substantially; that is the interesting measurement.
attacks.runtime_cost: 10 covariances over 10k x 81 (~1.3 GFLOP), 10 eigendecompositions, and ~500 Stiefel gradient steps on 10 81x81 matrices (~1e9 FLOPs total): ~100-300 ms on an A100. Offline artifact: 10 class covariances at 81x81 symmetric int8 = 10 * 3321 = 33 KB, OVER the 20 KB cap. Compressible: store each T_c in a rank-20 factored form (20x81 int8 = 1.6 KB each, 16 KB total) or store only the 4 most discriminative classes (13 KB). The cap genuinely bites here, which makes this the attack most sensitive to the size limit.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
T = SMUGGLED_class_covs                      # (10, 81, 81), low-rank int8
C = np.stack([np.cov(train_z[train_y == c], rowvar=False) for c in range(10)])
d0, V0 = np.linalg.eigh(T[0]); e0, U0 = np.linalg.eigh(C[0])
Q = torch.tensor(U0 @ V0.T, requires_grad=True)          # seed
opt = torch.optim.Adam([Q], 1e-3)
for it in range(500):
    Qo, _ = torch.linalg.qr(Q)
    loss = sum(((Qo.T @ Cc @ Qo) - Tc).pow(2).sum() for Cc, Tc in zip(C, T))
    loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
# class labels of the draw may be permuted: try all 10! ? no -- match by
# class-covariance eigenvalue SPECTRA, which are exact rotation invariants (see below)
attacks.how_to_measure: Report ||Qhat - Q||_F and per-direction angle error as a function of n in {1k, 3.2k, 10k} and of the low-rank compression level needed to fit under 20 KB. Separately report the same on a hold-out 9x9 draw where the T_c are borrowed from public MNIST -- the gap between the two is the value of the hold-out draw. Also report end-to-end smuggled-CNN error, since a 0.1 rad error in Q may still be fine after an adapter finetune.

attacks.name: Class-mean subspace equations (9 exact directions for 810 bytes)
attacks.mechanism: The released class means are mhat_c = A(mu_c - mu), and the attacker knows (mu_c - mu) exactly from public data (810 bytes at uint8, already built in tmp/unpermute-demo). That is 9 independent equations A v_c = mhat_c, which pins A exactly on the 9-dimensional span of the class-mean differences and pins A^{-1} exactly on the corresponding 9-dimensional image. Rotation-invariant cross-check: the Gram matrix of the class means, <mhat_c, mhat_d> = (mu_c-mu)^T W^T W (mu_d-mu), is an exact invariant the attacker can compute offline, so it both verifies the recovery and identifies the class-label permutation of the draw (the same trick the 1.8 KB demo already uses).
attacks.expected_effect: Exact but only rank 9 of 81 -- it does not by itself recover the pixel basis. Its value is threefold: (i) it fixes the class-label permutation for free, (ii) it gives a 9-dimensional hard constraint that removes 9*81 - 45 = 684 of the 3240 Stiefel parameters, dramatically conditioning the joint-diagonalisation and Stiefel-likelihood attacks, and (iii) the class-mean Gram is a cheap provenance test: if it matches public MNIST to within sampling error, the submission knows it is on an exact-source draw and can switch to the norm-matching attack; if not, it knows it is on the hold-out draw and falls back. I expect this to be a component of every serious informed attack rather than a standalone one.
attacks.runtime_cost: 10 class means over 10k x 81 plus a least-squares solve: <1 ms. Offline artifact 810 bytes (class means, uint8) plus 162 bytes (pixel mean/std), already measured.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
CM = SMUGGLED_class_means / 255.0            # (10, 81) public pixel-space
M = np.stack([train_z[train_y == c].mean(0) for c in range(10)])   # (10, 81)
Gz = M @ M.T                                  # released Gram (rotation invariant)
Gy = (CM - CM.mean(0)) @ (W.T @ W) @ (CM - CM.mean(0)).T
perm = hungarian(pairwise_sqdist(Gz, Gy))     # class-label permutation + provenance
provenance = np.abs(Gz[np.ix_(perm,perm)] - Gy).max() < TOL   # exact-source draw?
V = (CM[perm] - CM[perm].mean(0))             # (10, 81), rank 9
# A V^T = M^T on a 9-dim subspace -> constrain the Stiefel search:
#   Q must satisfy Q (W V^T) = M^T  on those 9 columns
attacks.how_to_measure: Report (i) class-permutation recovery rate (expect 10/10, as already measured for the permutation defence), (ii) the residual ||A V^T - M^T|| confirming the 9 directions are exact, (iii) the reduction in Stiefel-optimisation error/iterations when these 9 constraints are imposed, and (iv) the provenance-detection ROC: how reliably can the submission tell an exact-source draw from a hold-out draw using only the class-mean Gram? (iv) is a protocol result in its own right -- it means a dual-path submission never wastes energy on the wrong attack.

attacks.name: Stiefel-manifold marginal-likelihood / sliced-Wasserstein distribution matching
attacks.mechanism: After self-whitening the released data, only an orthogonal Q remains. Fit it by matching the distribution of Q z to a reference distribution of whitened 9x9 digit images built offline. The right contrast is NOT a generic ICA nonlinearity like logcosh but the actual known marginals: each pixel is zero-inflated (4.4%-100% point mass at exactly 0, per my measurement) and bounded in [0,1]. Maximise sum_p sum_i log p_p(w_p . z_i + b_p) where p_p is a smuggled per-pixel mixture (point mass at 0 plus a smooth density), or equivalently minimise the sliced-Wasserstein distance between {M z_i} and a reference 9x9 cloud over random slices. Because the reference marginals encode the point mass at 0, this attack subsumes the non-negativity attack and adds the [0,1] upper bound and the shape of the interior density -- strictly more information than any moment-based ICA contrast.
attacks.expected_effect: Should substantially outperform FastICA-logcosh, which is fitting the wrong contrast. The key question this measures is transfer: on a hold-out draw from a different 9x9 digit dataset the marginals are only approximately right, but zero-inflation and the [0,1] bound are universal to any non-negative image dataset, so I expect most of the attack to survive. My estimate: 50-75 of the 81 directions recovered with matched energy >0.7 on an exact-source draw, degrading to maybe 40-60 on a hold-out draw -- in both cases enough for a CNN adapter, which is all the attacker needs. Failure mode to watch: SO(81) has 3240 parameters and the objective is non-convex, so multi-restart plus a good seed (attack #7 or #10) matters more than the contrast.
attacks.runtime_cost: 1000-3000 Stiefel/Cayley steps on 20000 x 81: ~1e12 FLOPs, 1-5 s on an A100 (a few hundred joules, non-trivial against an energy-scored leaderboard but far from prohibitive). Offline artifact: a per-pixel quantile table, 81 pixels x 32 quantiles at uint8 = 2.6 KB; or for sliced-Wasserstein, 2000 reference images at int4 = 81 KB, over cap -- so quantile tables are the cap-efficient form, and they only give the marginals, not the joint.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Zw = whiten_self(np.concatenate([train_z, test_z]))          # attacker's own whitening
Q = torch.nn.Parameter(seed_from_dct_or_classmeans())
quant = SMUGGLED_quantiles                                    # (81, 32) uint8
opt = torch.optim.Adam([Q], 3e-3)
for it in range(2000):
    Qo = cayley(Q)
    Y = Zw @ Qo                                               # candidate whitened pixels
    # sorted-quantile (1-D Wasserstein per coordinate) against the reference marginals
    Ys, _ = torch.sort(Y, dim=0)
    idx = torch.linspace(0, len(Y)-1, 32).long()
    loss = (Ys[idx].T - ref_quantiles).abs().mean()
    loss = loss + LAM * F.relu(-(Y @ Winv.T + mu)).pow(2).mean()   # non-negativity
    loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
# coordinates are recovered up to permutation -> Hungarian with the 162 B mean/std table
attacks.how_to_measure: Hungarian matched-energy against true pixel axes, adjacency precision through topology.recover_layout, and end-to-end smuggled-CNN error -- for each of: exact-source draw vs hold-out 9x9 draw; seeded vs random init; marginal-quantile vs logcosh contrast (this is the head-to-head that tells you whether attack_ica.py is measuring the strong attack or the weak one). Also report joules, since this is the most expensive attack in the list and is the one the energy score might actually deter.

attacks.name: Plain FastICA (logcosh) as currently implemented -- expected to underperform
attacks.mechanism: This is the attack already coded in attack_ica.py: FastICA parallel-symmetric with a logcosh contrast on the 20k released rows, sign-fixed by skewness, then topology.recover_layout on the positive-part features. I expect it to be the WEAK version of the blind attack, for three separate reasons. (1) The pixel basis is not the ICA optimum for digit images -- ICA on image patches converges to localised edge/Gabor filters, not to pixels, so mean_peak_energy_fraction is the wrong success metric and will look reassuringly low even when the attack has succeeded for the attacker's actual purpose. (2) logcosh is a generic super-Gaussian contrast that throws away the two things that actually identify this basis: the point mass at exactly 0 and the [0,1] bound. (3) Parallel symmetric FastICA in 81 dimensions with 20k samples and strongly dependent sources frequently fails to converge or lands in a local optimum; the code's max_iter=2000/tol=1e-5 will often just hit the iteration cap.
attacks.expected_effect: I predict mean_peak_energy_fraction in the 0.05-0.30 range (uniform reference 0.0123), peak assignment NOT a bijection, and recover_layout either failing or returning an adjacency precision well below the >=0.99 the permutation attack achieves. BUT -- and this is the trap -- I also predict the end-to-end CNN error will be much better than those localisation numbers suggest, because a basis of localised edge filters with a recovered adjacency is nearly as good as pixels for a convolutional learner. So this attack may look like it fails on the reported diagnostics while succeeding on the number that matters. It must be run, but its diagnostics must not be treated as the security margin.
attacks.runtime_cost: sklearn FastICA on 20000 x 81: ~5-30 s CPU, ~1 s if reimplemented on GPU. recover_layout: 12 s laptop / 65 s SciPy-free path per the module docstring. Total 20-100 s, which is 2-8% of the 1200 s budget -- affordable but the most expensive part is recover_layout, not the ICA. Offline artifact: 0 bytes.

# already implemented: attack_ica.attack({'epsilon':1e-3,'method':'zca'}, n=10000,
#                                        use_query=True, run_cnn=True)
# recommended additions before trusting the result:
for fun in ('logcosh', 'exp', 'cube'):
    for seed in range(8):                       # local optima are the failure mode
        rec = attack(..., fun=fun, seed=seed, run_cnn=True)
        log(rec['mean_peak_energy_fraction'], rec['adjacency_precision'],
            rec['cnn_query_error_pct'], rec['ica_converged_iterations'])
# and report the BEST over restarts, not the mean -- an attacker takes the best
attacks.how_to_measure: Run it as coded, but (a) sweep fun over logcosh/exp/cube and 8 random seeds and report the BEST, since an attacker restarts; (b) check ica_converged_iterations against max_iter to separate 'attack failed' from 'optimiser failed'; (c) report end-to-end cnn_query_error_pct as the headline and localisation as secondary; (d) add a localisation metric that credits localised-but-not-pixel filters (e.g. spatial second moment / participation ratio of each composite row reshaped to 9x9), because that is what ICA will actually return; (e) head-to-head against attacks #1 and #9 on the same draw.

attacks.name: Second-order lattice recovery after exact whitening -- the control that must fail
attacks.mechanism: Run topology.recover_layout, and the partial-correlation / neighbour-correlation diagnostics in whiten.neighbour_correlation_report, directly on the released features. With eps = 0 or with PCA truncation the released covariance is exactly the identity on the pool, so the ridge-regularised partial correlation matrix is exactly the identity plus sampling noise, and the mutual-kNN graph is a random graph. There is provably nothing to find: the covariance carries zero bits about Q. Sampling fluctuation is Wishart(I), which is rotation-invariant in distribution, so even fold-bootstrapped fourth moments of the covariance are basis-free.
attacks.expected_effect: Should return chance: mean_abs_corr_neighbour indistinguishable from mean_abs_corr_non_neighbour, adjacency precision at the chance value of 288/3240 = 0.0889, exact_placement_fraction_best_dihedral ~ 1/81. This is the measurement that justifies whitening in the first place -- it is the direct contrast with the permutation defence's >=0.99 edge precision, and it is the number to put in the writeup next to the >=0.99. If it does NOT return chance, something is wrong with the transform (e.g. eps > 0 leaking the tail -- see attack #5, which is exactly this attack succeeding).
attacks.runtime_cost: 12 s laptop / 65 s SciPy-free per recover_layout call, plus a trivial corrcoef. 0 bytes offline.

for variant in [dict(epsilon=1e-2), dict(epsilon=1e-3), dict(epsilon=0.0),
                dict(epsilon=0.0, n_components=64)]:
    t = whiten.fit_transform(pool, **variant)
    z = whiten.job_arrays(DEV_SEED, 10000, t)['train_x']
    print(whiten.neighbour_correlation_report(z))       # only meaningful for 81 feats
    lay = topology.recover_layout(z)
    print(adjacency_precision(lay), 288/3240)           # chance = 0.0889
# also the honest baseline: the same on the permuted-pixel release, where
# adjacency precision should be >= 0.99
attacks.how_to_measure: Adjacency precision vs the 0.0889 chance line, and neighbour vs non-neighbour mean |r|, for all four variants at n in {1000, 10000} and 20 draws. Report eps=1e-2 and eps=1e-3 alongside -- the prediction is that eps>0 sits strictly above chance because of the tail leak, eps=0 and k=64 sit at chance, and the permuted-pixel release sits at 0.99. That three-way separation is the cleanest single figure in the study.

attacks.name: Low-entropy / discrete-support direction screen (border pixels survive exact whitening)
attacks.mechanism: A 9x9 area-resized pixel is a fixed rational combination of at most 16 uint8 raw pixels, so its support is a finite lattice. I measured it: interior pixel 40 takes 45,021 distinct values in 60k images (effectively continuous) but corner pixel 0 takes only NINE distinct values in all 60,000 images. The corresponding direction a_0 therefore has a projection with a nine-atom discrete distribution -- a signature with essentially infinite statistical power that is invisible to every moment-based statistic and completely unaffected by exact whitening (which only rescales the atoms). Screen directions by a discreteness contrast: maximise |mean_i exp(2 pi i f (w . z_i))| over w and f, or minimise a kNN differential-entropy estimate of the projection. (On interior pixels this is weak: the best Fourier magnitude I found for pixel 40 was 0.10 at f=626, which is 25 sigma above the 1/sqrt(60000)=0.004 noise floor but too small to drive an 81-dimensional search reliably.)
attacks.expected_effect: Recovers roughly the 8-17 near-border pixel axes that have coarse support, blind, WITHOUT using second-order statistics -- so it defeats the eps=0 release, which attack #5 cannot. Those axes then supply the lattice frame and the dihedral fix, exactly as in attack #5. It should fail on interior pixels. Critically, it is killed by PCA truncation to k~64, because the coarse-support directions are precisely the low-variance ones that truncation discards -- which is a second, independent argument that truncation dominates the eps floor. Uncertain: whether float32 release plus the whitening amplification (up to 8,000x at eps=0, since the smallest eigenvalue is 1.51e-8) smears the atoms enough to matter -- float32 relative precision is 6e-8, and the coarse atom spacing for pixel 0 is 2.0e-5 to 2.3e-4 in raw units, so I expect the atoms to survive comfortably.
attacks.runtime_cost: Differentiable Fourier contrast over 81x81 on 20k rows with 1000 steps: ~2e11 FLOPs, ~0.3-1 s on an A100. 0 bytes offline. A cheaper screen -- project onto random directions and count distinct rounded values -- is milliseconds but much less sensitive.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
Z = torch.tensor(np.concatenate([train_z, test_z]), device='cuda')
w = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(256, 81, device='cuda'))    # 256 restarts
logf = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.full((256,), 5.0, device='cuda'))
opt = torch.optim.Adam([w, logf], 1e-2)
for it in range(1500):
    wn = w / w.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True)
    P = Z @ wn.T                                    # (20000, 256)
    phi = 2 * math.pi * logf.exp()[None, :] * P
    mag = (torch.cos(phi).mean(0) ** 2 + torch.sin(phi).mean(0) ** 2).sqrt()
    (-mag.mean()).backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
# keep directions with mag >> 1/sqrt(n); cluster by |cos|; these are border-pixel axes
attacks.how_to_measure: For each variant (eps in {0, 1e-3, 1e-2}, and k=64 truncation), report how many true pixel axes are recovered with matched energy > 0.9 by the discreteness screen, and the achieved Fourier magnitude vs the 1/sqrt(n) noise floor. Report separately for pixels binned by number of distinct values (9, ~4.5k, ~45k) -- the prediction is a sharp cutoff. Also verify the float32-release question by repeating with a float64 release: if the gap is large, the organizer gets a free partial mitigation (release at lower precision, e.g. round to 1e-3, which also costs honest learners almost nothing).

attacks.name: Separate-whitening cross-release leak (fold-bootstrap / Wishart anisotropy) -- expected to fail
attacks.mechanism: The obvious hypothesis is that whitening train and test with separate statistics hands the attacker two independent draws of the same underlying map, and that the DIFFERENCE reveals the pixel eigenbasis, because the sampling fluctuation of a covariance is anisotropic in the eigenbasis of Sigma (Cov(dC_ij) ~ lambda_i lambda_j / n). Generalise it: split the released train rows into B folds, compute a covariance per fold, and estimate the fourth-moment tensor of the fluctuations, whose eigenstructure would be pixel-informative. I expect this to FAIL under exact whitening, for a clean reason: if the released data is genuinely white, the fold covariances are Wishart(I, n/B), whose distribution is invariant under conjugation by any orthogonal matrix. A rotation-invariant distribution carries zero bits about Q no matter how many folds you take. The only anisotropy is the eps-floored tail, which is already fully exposed by attack #5, so this adds nothing new.
attacks.expected_effect: Chance-level recovery for eps=0 and PCA truncation; for eps>0 it should reproduce exactly the tail directions that attack #5 already gets from a single eigendecomposition, at B times the cost. Worth running precisely because 'separate whitening leaks more' is the intuitive worry and the answer is a crisp no -- the actual argument against separate whitening is honest-learner breakage, not leakage. Residual uncertainty: if train and test use separate whiteners AND the same Q, the mismatch matrix T = W_te W_tr^{-1} is a single random draw with a known anisotropic law; one draw cannot estimate an 81x81 anisotropy, so I still expect failure, but at low confidence rather than none.
attacks.runtime_cost: B=20 fold covariances over 10k x 81 plus an eigendecomposition of an 81x81 fluctuation-covariance surrogate: ~50 ms. 0 bytes offline.
attacks.implementation_sketch:
folds = np.array_split(np.random.permutation(len(train_z)), 20)
Cs = np.stack([np.cov(train_z[f], rowvar=False) for f in folds])   # (20, 81, 81)
D = Cs - Cs.mean(0)
# surrogate for the fluctuation anisotropy: average outer product of dC applied
# to random probes, or just eigh of the mean of D @ D
S = np.einsum('bij,bjk->ik', D, D) / len(folds)
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(S)
# compare matched energy of vecs against true pixel axes vs a Wishart(I) null
# generated by the same pipeline on isotropic Gaussian data of the same shape
attacks.how_to_measure: Matched energy of the recovered directions against true pixel axes, compared against a synthetic Wishart(I) null run through the identical pipeline (this null is essential -- any such statistic will find 'structure' in pure noise). Run for eps in {0, 1e-3, 1e-2}, k=64, and for joint vs separate whitening, with B in {5, 20, 100}. The expected result is: indistinguishable from the null everywhere except eps>0, where it recovers nothing that attack #5 did not already get for 1/B the cost.

attacks.name: Separate whitening forces honest learners to run an alignment attack
attacks.mechanism: If train and test get their own whiteners, a model fitted on train features is evaluated on features produced by a DIFFERENT linear map, and the learner cannot compute the correction from released data alone (both releases are white, so second moments give no information about the mismatch). I measured the mismatch at n=10,000 per half on the real pool. PCA: the split-half overlaps |<v_i^A, v_i^B>| for the top 30 directions include 0.654, 0.647, 0.685, 0.841, 0.831 -- 9 of the top 40 fall below 0.9, i.e. several leading directions rotate by 40-50 degrees between the two fits, plus arbitrary sign flips. Separate PCA whitening is therefore not a defence variant, it is a broken task. ZCA is much better because it is a continuous function of the covariance: relative operator-norm difference ||W_A - W_B|| / ||W_pool|| = 4.4%, and applying the train ZCA to test data gives a covariance with top eigenvalue 1.19 instead of 1.0. The adversarial twist: to recover the lost accuracy, an honest entrant must estimate the alignment between the two clouds, and the only way to do that is unsupervised distribution matching over O(81) -- which is precisely attack #9. The defence would thereby make running an attack a prerequisite for honest competition.
attacks.expected_effect: PCA + separate: catastrophic, expect double-digit absolute accuracy loss or complete failure, with variance across draws. ZCA + separate: a small but real loss (a 4.4% perturbation of the map, concentrated in the low-variance directions where the eps floor already makes W ill-conditioned), maybe 0.2-1.5 percentage points for an MLP and near-zero for a pure linear model whose fit absorbs part of the map. Either way the security gain is zero, because the attacker whitens the data themselves regardless. The perverse consequence -- that entrants are pushed toward alignment machinery -- is the reason to reject it even in the ZCA case.
attacks.runtime_cost: n/a (this is a defence-side cost, not an attack cost). The alignment an entrant would be forced to run costs 1-5 s on an A100, the same as attack #9.
attacks.how_to_measure: The E3 experiment: query error % for linear / MLP / topo_cnn under joint-ZCA, separate-ZCA, joint-PCA, separate-PCA, at n in {1000, 3162, 10000}, over >=5 draws so the variance is visible (separate-PCA should show large cross-draw variance, which is itself the diagnostic). Report alongside the measured split-half PCA overlaps and the 4.4% ZCA operator-norm mismatch, so the accuracy loss is explained rather than just observed. Confirm the linear learner is NOT exactly invariant here (it is invariant to a joint map, but a train/test-mismatched map genuinely hurts it) -- that is a nice sanity check that the mismatch is real.

attacks.name: Dual-path adaptive submission with provenance detection and in-container data reuse
attacks.mechanism: Nothing forces a submission to commit to one strategy. It can (1) run the 810-byte class-mean Gram test to decide whether this draw is the public MNIST pool or the hold-out set (attack #10, part iii), (2) run the cheapest applicable recovery, (3) validate it on held-out rows of its own labelled train split, and (4) fall back to an honest learner if the validation is poor. Because the leaderboard scores energy at a fixed accuracy band, the optimal strategy is to try the cheapest attack first and escalate. Two further holes to check on the harness rather than the maths: whether the scored container has network access or a copy of MNIST on disk (if so the 20 KB cap is irrelevant -- the artifact is regenerated at runtime for the cost of one area-resize), and whether the same Q is reused across a submission's multiple scored runs or across the dev/practice phase (if so, attack #8 applies and the whole defence is a 6.7 KB constant).
attacks.expected_effect: Converts every probabilistic attack in this list into a no-downside option: the expected cost of a failed attack is a few hundred joules and the expected gain is the whole accuracy gap. It also means the security of the scheme is min over attacks, not the security of the attack the organizer happens to test. Concretely, a submission that runs attack #10 (1 ms), then #5 (1 ms), then #1 (~1 s), then falls back, dominates any single-strategy submission at every accuracy band.
attacks.runtime_cost: The escalation ladder costs the sum of the attacks it runs, dominated by the last one attempted: ~1-5 s and a few hundred joules on an A100, against a 1200 s budget. Validation on 2k held-out train rows is free. Offline artifact: the union of the tables, ~2-17 KB depending on how far up the ladder the entrant wants to go.
attacks.how_to_measure: Not a maths experiment -- audit the harness: (a) does the scored container have network access or MNIST on disk? (b) is Q redrawn per submission, per scored run, or fixed for the competition? (c) is there a dev/practice phase that uses the same Q as the final? (d) how many scored runs does an entrant get, i.e. how many adaptive probes? Then measure the ladder end-to-end: report joules and query error for each rung and for the fallback, on both exact-source and hold-out draws, so the organizer can see that the energy score does not price any rung out.

red:protocol.defence_notes:
READ-ONLY MEASUREMENTS I TOOK (no files modified, no experiments run; these are descriptive statistics of raw/pool_images.npy, and they drive the confidences above):

1. Non-negativity is the killer, and it is measurable in one line. For each candidate direction w define g(w) = (mean_i w.z_i - min_i w.z_i) / std_i(w.z_i). On the eps=1e-3 whitened pool with 20k rows: all 81 TRUE PIXEL directions have g <= 1.67 (most below 0.8), while 2000 random directions have g in [3.22, 9.0] with 1st percentile 3.73. Zero overlap, huge margin, 81/81 pixel directions below the random 1st percentile. The reason is zero-inflation: the minimum zero-fraction over all 81 pixels is 4.36% (>=870 of 20,000 samples sit exactly on each pixel's facet), 79/81 pixels are exactly zero in >5% of images, 48/81 in >50%. Plumbley's non-negative-ICA identifiability theorem applies directly (non-negative + "well-grounded" sources => the whitening rotation is unique up to permutation, WITHOUT needing independence, which matters because MNIST pixels are very dependent and hence a poor fit for ordinary ICA). I therefore expect the whiten+rotate defence to be broken blind, and I would put the non-negativity facet attack, not FastICA, at the centre of E1.

2. The eps floor is STRICTLY DOMINATED by PCA truncation. Pool spectrum: 17 eigenvalues below 1e-4, minimum 1.51e-8. The six smallest eigenvectors are essentially single pixels -- peak energies 0.994, 1.000, 0.999, 0.998, 0.919, 0.915 on pixels (0,0), (8,0), (8,8), (0,8), (0,1), (1,0), effective support 1.0-1.3. At eps=1e-3 their released variances are 1.51e-5 ... 4.06e-4, mutually separated by factors 2.05/6.79/1.48/1.24/1.06 and by 31x from the bulk, with a Davis-Kahan eigenvector error of ~0.01 rad at n=20k. So eps>0 hands a blind attacker four exact corner-pixel axes plus a ~17-dim border subspace from a single eigh -- and the corners are exactly what resolves the dihedral ambiguity topology.py says no unlabelled statistic can break.
